items.title: Attack on Catholic Bishops is attack on entire Church, PFN fumes
items.description: •Vows to break bus preaching law By Olayinka Latona The National President of the Pentecostal Fellowship of Nigeria, PFN, Bishop Wale Oke, has thrown the full weight of the Pentecostal body behind the Catholic Bishops Conference of Nigeria, declaring that any attack on the Catholic bishops is an attack on the entire Body of Christ. Speaking during an interview monitored by Sunday Vanguard, Bishop Oke endorsed the remarks made by John Onaiyekan during the recent visit of the Catholic Bishops Conference of Nigeria, CBCN, to President Bola Tinubu, where the group told the President that “Nigeria is bleeding.” “Are we not bleeding? Are we not bleeding in Benue? Are we not bleeding in Southern Kaduna? Are we not bleeding in Gwoza, in Borno State? Are we not bleeding in Kwara? Are we not bleeding in Oyo State?” Oke queried, reiterating the Cardinal’s words verbatim. The PFN President challenged the government’s pushback against the bishops, insisting that speaking the truth to power is not a political act but a moral imperative. “Should anybody attack a Catholic bishop for saying that? That is the obvious truth,” he stated firmly. Bishop Oke dismissed attempts to isolate the Catholic bishops, emphasising Christian unity across denominations. “The Church of Jesus Christ is one. There may be many denominations, but we have one faith, one Lord, one baptism. The Church is one. If they attack the Catholic bishops, they are attacking the whole Church,” he declared. Plateau, Benue The PFN leader used the platform to condemn what he described as the government’s silence in the face of escalating violence against Christians, citing ongoing killings in Plateau, Southern Kaduna, Benue, Taraba, and recent incursions into Oyo, Kwara and Edo states by violent groups he linked to Islamic extremism. On the controversy surrounding the proposed amendment to the FRSC Act that would fine bus preachers ¦ 50,000, Bishop Oke was unequivocal. Despite the Senate’s clarification that the provision had existed since 2007 and was merely re-itemised, Oke insisted it must be expunged entirely. “We will break that law. Dear Senate of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, we will rather obey God than man,” he declared, adding that he has preached in buses since 1975 without causing any accident or distraction. “If you want to imprison us for preaching the gospel, we are ready. If you want to make all the stadiums in Nigeria prisons, we are ready. We would rather obey God than man,” he said defiantly. OIC withdrawal Beyond the bus preaching ban, Oke called on the National Assembly to address more fundamental issues, including Nigeria’s membership of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), which he said the country entered under military rule without the people’s consent. “The Senate should deal with that and pull Nigeria out of the OIC,” he demanded. He also renewed calls for a review of the 1999 Constitution, alleging it is skewed in favour of Islam. “In that Constitution, Islam is mentioned hundreds of times. Christianity is mentioned once. And Christians in Nigeria are a little over 50 per cent of the population,” he argued, insisting that the document was imposed by the “military jackboot” and does not represent the will of Nigerians. Genocide Bishop Oke doubled down on allegations of Christian genocide, accusing the government of spending billions to lobby against such claims in the United States while the killings continue. He distinguished between the primary targeting of Christians and the secondary killing of liberal Muslims who oppose extremist ideologies. “The Senate should invite the Church for a talk. Nigerians are being killed. You are sitting there making evil laws. We will break that law,” he concluded, reaffirming that the PFN is making private overtures to the Presidency even as it speaks publicly, though he declined to disclose details of those engagements. Timing Also, Pastor Seyi Osuntayo, Area Superintendent of The Apostolic Church Nigeria, Igbein Area, weighed in on the controversy, expressing concern about what he termed the “altercation” between the Presidency and the Catholic bishops. “The timing of the Catholic Bishops Conference of Nigeria’s advice could be suspicious and be seen as partisan,” Pastor Osuntayo told our correspondent. “I feel the Catholic Bishops should have been talking about governance ab initio, not at the time of the electioneering campaign,” he noted. The cleric, who maintains that Christian leaders should not be involved in “political roforofo” but should focus on governance, cited the biblical instruction in 1 Timothy 2:1–4, urging Christians to pray for leaders regardless of their performance. “Our leaders need prayer, whether we agree with their views and leadership style or not. We may not get to choose our leader or their position on the issues we care about, but we can choose to be obedient to the Lord and cover them in prayer,” Osuntayo said. He cautioned against the increasing trend of Christian leaders creating media content or participating in news coverage to criticise the government, arguing that such actions only add to the political heat. “Instead of complaining or criticising, we can surrender our emotions and let the power of prayer take over. We never saw Jesus calling people to activism or rebellion against the Roman leaders who would ultimately kill Him,” he added. Political hypocrisy However, Ben Charles-Davies, a journalist and author, dismissed what he described as the government’s attempt to divert attention from the real issues. “My simple response to the verbal exchange between the Presidency and the Catholic Bishops Conference of Nigeria is that it is unnecessary. The government is trying to divert attention from the main issue, which is poverty in the land,” Charles-Davies stated. He pointed to what he called “rank hypocrisy” in the government’s response, recalling that in November 2014, the CBCN, under the same Cardinal Onaiyekan, spoke against then-President Goodluck Jonathan’s administration’s handling of the economy. At the time, the opposition All Progressives Congress, APC, applauded and celebrated the cleric for being the voice of the voiceless. “Today, the APC government is angry because the same bishops informed them that Nigerians are going through socio-economic hardship and they are unhappy. That’s hypocrisy,” Charles-Davies asserted. He challenged government spokespersons to be more circumspect in attacking statesmen who hold contrary views, emphasising that “Nigeria belongs to all of us, not just those in government.” He further questioned the sincerity of government officials, asking: “Who in government, among ministers and advisers, can boldly tell the President the true situation of things in the country? Daily killings, kidnapping for ransom, food inflation, high transportation costs, collapsed health services, etc.? Not one. All of them are struggling to impress the President. Everything is going well. Nigerians are happy with the reforms.” He added that Cardinal Onaiyekan had simply expressed the feelings, pains and suffering of most Nigerians, regardless of their faith. Allegiance Ugoji Maximillian, a speaker, author and entrepreneur who was raised Catholic and attended a seminary, offered a more political analysis of the situation. “The Catholic bishops are a strong body. But they are highly political. They know how to play politics and can intimidate and threaten a politician using their structures,” Maximillian said. Maximillian, who claimed extensive knowledge of Catholic Church politics, gave a more controversial perspective, accusing the bishops of playing politics and attempting to intimidate the President. He traced the Church’s political influence across various states, citing examples of how Catholic clerics have shaped political outcomes in Enugu, Anambra, Imo, Benue and Kaduna states. “In 2023, they made a wrong move. That wrong move backfired. They put their eggs in one basket. They went all out for Peter Obi. They showed clearly that they disliked Tinubu. But they masked it by saying they were against the Muslim-Muslim ticket,” he added. The commentator argued that the bishops were “simply pursuing and supporting a candidate they felt was their boy, who would listen to them,” adding: “It pains influential men to be ignored by the one who rules their domains.” Economic progress On his part, a former Commissioner for Physical Planning in Lagos State, Mr Toyin Ayinde, offered a more nuanced perspective, suggesting that Nigerians have unrealistic expectations of change. “Politicians visiting a politician, and you want me to comment, especially when the former had openly shown, before the 2023 election, that they were pitched against the latter?” Ayinde questioned. He pointed to what he described as tangible economic progress, noting that his naira ATM card, which was previously unusable for online transactions, could now be used for purchases abroad. “I have, in the course of this year, made an online payment of about £4,500 using my naira ATM card, and while in Canada, I used my naira ATM card for most of my purchases. I didn’t need to use the dollar card.” Ayinde cautioned that “Nigerians don’t understand process, so everything must happen at microwave speed,” adding that the country is “heavily soaked in the culture of shaming.” “Rather than contribute advice for a guided way forward, we look for what to talk about in a disrespectful way to shame the other party,” he said. The post Attack on Catholic Bishops is attack on entire Church, PFN fumes appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: SMOKERS’ CORNER: THE OUTRAGE MACHINE
items.description: A short video recently circulating on social media shows Adolf Hitler drinking from a can of Fanta while angrily proclaiming, “I hate juice.” Though millions mistook it for an authentic commercial, sparking fierce online debate, it is actually an AI-generated meme. Its artificial nature is fairly obvious, given that the colour, fonts and logo on the can look nothing like actual Fanta packaging. So why did so many people fall for it? The answer lies in our current media topography, where “shockvertising” has been methodically normalised. The term ‘shockvertising’ emerged in the early 1990s, though the practice dates back to public health campaigns in the late 1960s, and describes a marketing strategy that deliberately violates social, moral or aesthetic boundaries to startle, offend or disturb an audience. Unlike traditional advertisements that highlight product benefits, shockvertising relies on instinctive reactions like fear, disgust, horror or outrage to cut through commercial noise. This is done to drive high brand recall and generate free publicity. Due to the fact that real brands have pushed boundaries in the recent past, a concept as absurd as a Hitler-themed Fanta advertisement suddenly felt plausible to an over-stimulated public. In an online world where algorithms reward anger over accuracy, outrage has become one of the most valuable forms of currency in the digital age The earliest examples of shockvertising emerged in the late 1960s and early 1970s through Western government funded anti-smoking campaigns, which featured graphic images of diseased lungs. While these visuals shocked audiences, the public largely accepted them because they served the purpose of raising awareness about smoking-related illnesses. Eventually, governments made it a legal requirement for tobacco companies to print these graphic images directly on cigarette packets. Seeing how receptive people were to shocking imagery when tied to a meaningful cause, and recognising its power to ignite widespread public debate, several consumer brands decided to adopt similar tactics to shatter the clutter of traditional advertising. In the late 1980s, Italian clothing brand United Colours of Benetton transformed shockvertising into a corporate strategy. Instead of displaying clothes, Benetton ran controversial photographs of a dying AIDS activist, a priest kissing a nun and blood-soaked war uniforms, linking the brand directly to concentrated social debates. Luxury brands such as Gucci and Tom Ford later introduced hyper-sexualised, taboo imagery to build an ‘edgy’, exclusive identity, often actively courting media bans to secure free publicity. Illustration by Abro Modern shock tactics have since migrated online, leaning heavily into ‘rage-baiting’ and controversial social stances engineered specifically to drive viral outrage, heated debate and clicks across digital platforms. Shockvertising is an offshoot of what is often referred to as the “outrage economy.” American media theorists Tim Wu and Shoshana Zuboff describe the outrage economy as a digital marketplace where human attention is monetised through heightened conflict and anger. Rather than promoting a brand on its merits or presenting a topic through objective analysis, the outrage economy banks on manufactured outrage to bypass critical thinking, instantly capturing attention and high digital traffic through viral sharing and continuous debate. Social media ‘influencers’ and vloggers frequently resort to making absurd claims and spreading outright falsehoods, purely to inflate their views and comment sections. Far from discouraging this behaviour, social media platforms reward it. Their underlying algorithms are engineered to prioritise high engagement above truth, effectively monetising outrageous content and turning controversy into a business model. Pakistani comedian Tabish Hashmi recently sparked widespread online debate by announcing his departure from a Geo TV show that he hosts. Disappointed fans quickly flooded social media platforms, but their dismay rapidly morphed into outrage after a rumour surfaced claiming Hashmi had been fired over controversial remarks regarding political unrest in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK). Remarkably, those expressing outrage rarely paused to verify the nature, or even the existence, of the supposed comments. In reality, no such statements were ever made. The entire episode was a staged publicity stunt. Hashmi was never asked to leave and Geo TV had merely paused production briefly to redesign the show’s set. For days, however, the host and the programme dominated digital discourse. The manufactured controversy allowed observers to project their own political narratives on to the event, with some reading complex state conspiracies into the hiatus and others extending outrage over perceived censorship. The situation raises certain questions about this strategy. Did Geo need to engineer a hoax to boost lagging ratings? But more amusing was the swiftness with which Geo and Hashmi ultimately dismissed the incident as a harmless “prank”. This may suggest a sudden loss of nerve once the audience transformed a routine promotional stunt into a tense conversation about free speech and anti-establishment rhetoric. After the hoax was revealed, many felt disappointed, and even embarrassed, at having been so easily duped. Yet, this vulnerability to manipulation is no longer an anomaly. In an era dominated by swift digital communication and heightened emotional engagement, such impressionability has ceased to be an exception. It has become the standard condition of the modern audience. The media in general and brands are aware of this. It has become easy for manufactured outrage to profit from growing gullibility. When digital platforms actively reward sensationalism over accuracy, critical thinking takes a back seat to knee-jerk reactions. As a result, audiences have grown increasingly susceptible to manufactured narratives, routinely accepting outrage at face value before taking the time to verify basic facts. Politicians, corporate brands, influencers, vloggers, mainstream media outlets and even everyday users all feed this cycle. It is no wonder, then, that the concept of online “trending topics” has so seamlessly replaced genuine public discourse, turning meaningful dialogue into an algorithmic spectacle. To paraphrase the American media theorist Neil Postman, the spectacle is designed for consumption rather than comprehension. Published in Dawn, EOS, August 9th, 2026

items.title: Six months in captivity: Woro freed victims recount ordeal
items.description: •Young women married off •Some male captives joined terrorists’ camp •OFFICIAL: Survivors tested positive to acute malaria fever, malnutrition By Demola Akinyemi Six months after they were abducted by terrorists, survivors of the Woro community attack in Kaiama Local Government Area of Kwara State have recounted the harrowing experiences they endured in captivity, including the deaths of 13 children, forced marriages involving some young women and severe hunger and deprivation. The victims were abducted on February 3, 2026, when terrorists attacked the community. The survivors, who were rescued by security forces and officially handed over to the Kwara State Government on Friday, narrated their ordeal while meeting with Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq in Ilorin. Meanwhile, medical examinations conducted on the released victims have revealed that some of them tested positive for acute malaria and malnutrition. Sunday Vanguard gathered that selected officials of the Kwara State Ministry of Health commenced intensive medical examinations on the remaining released victims at a designated hotel in the Government Reserved Area, GRA, Ilorin, where they are being accommodated. Fourteen of the victims, whose conditions were said to be critical when they arrived in Ilorin on Thursday night, have been transferred to the Kwara State University Teaching Hospital, Ilorin, for further medical attention. A source in the Ministry of Health, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the tests conducted so far showed that some of the victims were suffering from acute malaria and malnutrition. Asked about the possible causes of the conditions, the official said: “We only treated them based on the results we obtained after carrying out the tests. Ours is not to ask them questions about the environment they lived in or how they were treated.” Recounting her experience, one of the survivors, Ameerah Saliu, said she assisted in delivering 11 pregnant women while in captivity, but only about half of the babies survived. Ameerah, who identified herself as a health worker, said she had to rely on her professional knowledge to assist the pregnant women despite the harsh conditions in the terrorists’ camp. “It was like living in hell and striving to stay alive. At one point, all hope was lost, but thanks to Almighty Allah, freedom eventually came. “I’m a health worker, so I just had to assist the women to deliver. I delivered, I think, about 11 babies, but only half of them survived due to the terrible and harsh environment,” she said. She disclosed that 13 children died in the camp as a result of the harsh conditions, while some young women were married off and some young men eventually joined the terrorists’ camp. “Ultimately, 13 children died due to the very bad conditions, and the experience was quite harrowing, seeing their death and burial,” she said. According to her, the women were not sexually molested during their captivity, but they were subjected to severe hunger and deprivation. “We were fed with anything, like kulikuli, and given any water, maybe once in a day, just to keep whoever could stay alive,” she said. Ameerah said the victims had almost lost hope of regaining their freedom before their eventual rescue. She expressed appreciation to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, the Kwara State Government and the security agencies for securing their freedom. Another survivor, Hauwa Saliu, one of the wives of the Woro village head, corroborated Ameerah’s account, describing their experience in captivity as one that was difficult to put into words. “None of us believed we would ever be freed again, and so we resigned to fate. Interestingly, they pray too, but Almighty Allah is merciful. Those experiences can’t be recounted. But we are happy for freedom today,” she said. Receiving the victims, Governor AbdulRazaq commended President Tinubu and the security agencies for the successful rescue operation. He described the operation as a demonstration of the Federal Government’s commitment to protecting lives and restoring peace to communities affected by terrorism and banditry. The governor assured the survivors of the state government’s continued support, rehabilitation and reintegration. He said government would continue to provide the necessary assistance to help the victims recover from the trauma and challenges associated with their prolonged captivity. Sunday Vanguard gathered that 46 of the rescued survivors are currently receiving medical treatment at the Kwara State University Teaching Hospital The post Six months in captivity: Woro freed victims recount ordeal appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Infantino denies allegations of affair, favouritism while at UEFA
items.description: PARIS: FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who has endured a week of scathing criticism revolving around the now shelved private investment plan, has been accused by a British newspaper of paying off an alleged lover while at UEFA. According to The Telegraph , the Italian-Swiss lawyer, who served as secretary general of European football’s governing body from 2009 to 2016, also previously used his influence to secure a promotion for the same UEFA employee with whom he was in an intimate relationship. Infantino has categorically denied the allegations, according to the article which was published late on Friday. When contacted by AFP on Saturday, a FIFA spokesperson had not responded. According to The Telegraph , which did not cite its sources, this employee received a “a six-figure sum” upon her departure — at an unspecified time — in addition to the payment of tuition fees for a business school amounting to around 45,000 ($60,700). When contacted by AFP , UEFA acknowledged that “a departure payment was made to the individual in question” at that time, “coupled with the payment of fees for an MBA course at a local business school”. However, it insisted “the payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time”, before adding that “such regulations have been tightened since 2016”. Quoted by The Telegraph , a FIFA spokesperson stated that Infantino, who has been married since 2001, “strongly denies these allegations”, which were “categorically untrue”. “Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory,” FIFA added. “No employee at UEFA and FIFA has ever raised a complaint regarding Infantino’s behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved.” Infantino, who is standing for re-election next March, has been embroiled in a crisis since the announcement late last month of his controversial — and ultimately abandoned — plan to open up the World Cup to private investors. He faces opposition in particular from UEFA, which on Thursday stood by its threat to boycott the World Cups, deeming the mere withdrawal of the controversial plan to be insufficient. Published in Dawn, August 9th, 2026

items.title: Nigeria may lose out on fresh $1.4bn US health aid over Christians persecution
items.description: By Nkiruka Nnorom Nigeria may be excluded from a new $1.4 billion U.S health and humanitarian assistance package announced earlier this week if the Federal Government fails to take measurable actions to address violence against Christians, according to terms contained in a bilateral Memorandum of Understanding signed by both countries. The MOU, signed on December 20, 2025 between the U.S Department of State and the Nigerian government under the America First Global Health Strategy, AFGHS, commits Washington to nearly $2.1 billion over five years to expand preventative and curative services for HIV, TB, malaria, maternal and child health and polio. Under the MoU, Nigeria is also expected to increase its domestic health spending by nearly $3 billion during the term, an expenditure that has been described as the largest co-investment under AFGHS. A significant portion of the U.S funding is earmarked for Nigeria’s 900 faith-based clinics and hospitals, which currently serve more than 30 percent of Nigerians.However, the deal contains strict conditions. The MOU states that the agreement was “negotiated in connection with reforms the Nigerian government has made to prioritize protecting Christian populations from violence” and includes “significant dedicated funding” for Christian health facilities. Crucially, it adds: “As with all foreign assistance, the President and Secretary of State retain the right to pause or terminate any programme which do not align with the national interest, and the Trump administration expects Nigeria to continue to make progress ensuring that it combats extremist religious violence against vulnerable Christian populations.” The conditionality was reinforced by the U.S House of Representatives, which recently voted to tie Nigeria’s aid to verifiable steps on tackling Christian persecution. The bill passed last month by the House of Rep tasked Abuja with taking concrete actions to ensure the return of internally displaced persons to their ancestral homes and ensuring protection for persecuted Christians in the Middle Belt region among others. Meanwhile, in the fresh aid approved by Washington under its AFGHS, the U.S set aside $1.4 billion to support integrated health services through faith and community-based hospitals and clinics in more than 20 countries. Out of it, $850 million will go through a Faith and Community Initiative Award to World Vision and local faith-based implementers to strengthen over 2,500 faith-based hospitals and clinics across 17 countries with more than 30,000 community health workers trained, paid, and equipped. An additional $570 million will be channeled directly to faith-based and community hospitals through bilateral MOUs with governments, including Nigeria. In humanitarian assistance, the State Department also announced $538 million for Samaritan’s Purse and a World Vision–Compassion International consortium to reach 7 million people across 16 humanitarian crises. Over $100 million will be made immediately available for disaster response in 23 disaster-prone countries. The State Department said the combined $1.4 billion health announcement is the largest to faith-based organizations in over 20 years, with at least 80 percent of resources required to go directly to frontline services. For Nigeria, the MOU specifically emphasized support for Christian faith-based health care providers, which are described in the agreement as “uniquely positioned” to complement public facilities. With the U.S shifting more resources to faith-based delivery where such providers account for 40 per cent or more of health facilities in many aid-recipient countries, Nigeria’s access to the new funding will depend on how Abuja addresses concerns raised in Washington. The State Department said partners like Samaritan’s Purse, World Vision and Compassion International were chosen for their record of rapid deployment in conflict zones and disaster areas without bureaucratic delay. The post Nigeria may lose out on fresh $1.4bn US health aid over Christians persecution appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: OSUN VIOLENCE: We’re the victims, Adeleke is playing victim to curry sympathy – Oyebamiji
items.description: By Adetutu Oyebanjo Governorship candidate of the All Progressives Congress, APC, in Osun State, Biodun Oyebamiji, has accused Governor Ademola Adeleke of playing the victim to curry sympathy ahead of Saturday’s governorship poll. Adeleke has repeatedly accused the APC of attacking his administration and members of his party, Accord Party, to instill fear ahead of the election. Meanwhile, Oyebamiji denied the accusation, saying he and other members of the APC were the true victims of political violence in the state. Addressing newsmen, the former Chief Executive Officer of the National Inland Waterways Authority, NIWA, also accused the ruling party of killing several members of the state’s APC from 2023 to date. His words: “We are the victims. The governor is just playing the victim to curry sympathy. In his mind, he knows the truth. Therefore, let me seize this opportunity to reassure Osun people and Nigerians, through you, that both the APC and I are the real victims of persistent political violence in Osun State. “During the 2022 governorship election, more than 25 members of our party were murdered by members of the political party in power in Osun. In my own local government area for example, the Chairman of Irewole Local Government Area, Remi Abass, was killed within the council secretariat last year. “From 2023 to date, several of our members and other Osun citizens have been killed by agents of government. Our party has also documented several other politically motivated attacks and killings, for which we continue to seek justice through the courts. Therefore, the ongoing political violence has all the signs of government in power on it. Just recently, the Inspector-General of Police visited Osun State and publicly raised allegations concerning individuals accused of criminal activities being housed within the Government House. Recent reports indicate that some of our members were attacked in Ede, the hometown of Governor Adeleke. As an opposition party, these are some of the experiences of members of our party. Ironically, it is the Accord Party and government of Adeleke that are crying foul while our members bear the scars of political violence.” On his plans if elected, he said: “Once the good people of Osun hand me the mandate, we will, in line with our campaign promises, within our first 100 days in office, undertake a comprehensive review of all outstanding entitlements owed to active and retired workers and commence immediate payment. We are equally committed to to ensuring that the Dagbolu Dry Port becomes fully operational. In addition to these, through strategic partnerships, we will commence the training and empowerment of no fewer than 10,000 young people in information and communication technology. We will also institutionalise monthly monthly meetings of the State Security Council involving security agencies, traditional rulers and local government leaders.” The post OSUN VIOLENCE: We’re the victims, Adeleke is playing victim to curry sympathy – Oyebamiji appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Another Lagos bridge badly vandalised as Sanwo-Olu allays safety concerns
items.description: By Olasunkanmi Akoni LAGOS — Another bridge in Lagos has allegedly been vandalised, with a section of the concrete protection of an overhead bridge around Mile 12 reportedly excavated to expose reinforced iron rods, raising fresh concerns over the safety of critical public infrastructure in the state. The development came barely after residents raised the alarm over the alleged vandalisation of the Alakija-Festac Link Bridge, where suspected scavengers were accused of breaking the concrete covering of some bridge pillars and removing iron reinforcements. The latest incident, captured in a viral video, reportedly showed a suspected vandal caught in the act by vigilant residents, who expressed concern over the growing activities of scavengers targeting bridges and other public infrastructure for their iron components. Residents urged relevant authorities to intervene immediately to prevent further damage, warning that continued vandalism could compromise public infrastructure and expose road users to danger. They also called for increased security and surveillance around bridges and other public assets across the metropolis to curb the activities of vandals and scavengers. The Mile 12 incident came as Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu yesterday inspected the vandalised section of the Alakija-Festac Link Bridge and allayed fears over its structural safety. Sanwo-Olu, who conducted an on-the-spot assessment of the affected bridge pillar at Vin-Niger, along the Lagos-Badagry Expressway, assured residents and motorists that preliminary assessment showed that the bridge remained structurally sound and safe for use. The governor, however, declared a manhunt for those behind the vandalism and warned individuals involved in buying and selling stolen public infrastructure materials that government would pursue them. The Alakija-Festac Link Bridge, constructed by the Federal Housing Authority, FHA, links the Ojo axis with Festac Town and serves as an important route for motorists and pedestrians. The governor’s inspection followed a viral video circulating on social media at the weekend, in which a resident drew the attention of authorities to the alleged damage to the bridge. The resident accused scavengers of breaking the concrete covering of the bridge pillars and extracting the iron rods inside, warning that continued excavation could compromise the structure. He said: “This is the bridge that was constructed all the way from Alakija to link inside Festac. These scavengers have started removing iron from the pillars that support the bridge. Reacting to the incident, Sanwo-Olu said the land and abutment of the bridge were under the control of the FHA, adding that the main structure remained intact despite the vandalism. According to him, vandals had excavated and removed some fittings used to secure the facility, but the preliminary assessment did not indicate any compromise to the structural integrity of the bridge. He described the development as “unacceptable” and vowed to go after those responsible, including persons who facilitate the criminal trade by purchasing stolen public infrastructure materials. Meanwhile, 30 suspected vandals were arraigned before a Mobile Magistrate Court sitting at Bolade, Oshodi, Lagos, for allegedly vandalising and removing iron rods supporting the Alakija-Festac Link Bridge, Trade Fair, Orile and Abule Ado bridges. The suspects pleaded guilty to the charges and were subsequently convicted and sentenced to two months imprisonment each by the court. Reacting to the development, the Corps Marshal of the Kick Against Indiscipline, KAI, Major Olawale Cole, retd., said the agency remained determined to rid Lagos State of criminal elements through sustained enforcement. Cole said the conviction would serve as a warning to others involved in the vandalisation of public infrastructure, adding that KAI would continue to collaborate with relevant agencies to protect government property across the state. The post Another Lagos bridge badly vandalised as Sanwo-Olu allays safety concerns appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: New autopsy finds Mir Ali Raza was shot in the back, suffered multiple injuries
items.description: • Eight-member board exhumed the corpse in presence of magistrate, family • Police surgeon says cause of death reserved till receipt of reports • Says young businessman suffered injuries on head and face • Family lawyer wants investigation team replaced KARACHI: A fresh post-mortem examination conducted following the exhumation of the body of young business owner Mir Ali Raza on Saturday found that he had been shot in the back, evidence that ruled out the possibility of suicide. Sources told Dawn that an eight-member medical board that exhumed the body in the presence of a judicial magistrate at the Tariq Road graveyard also found “multiple injuries on the head and face” and “fractures on the nasal bone and skull” that indicated he might have been subjected to torture before being fatally shot. Raza, owner of eatery Wafflix, had gone missing on July 28. The 25-year-old’s body was found a day later with a gunshot wound in bushes near Shahi Qila Ground in Gulistan-i-Jauhar. While his family is convinced that he was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, investigators probing the incident said they found evidence that strengthened the possibility that he died by suicide. A controversy over flawed autopsy report and investigations compelled Raza’s family to file an application before a judicial magistrate for exhumation of the body for a fresh post-mortem examination. On Saturday, the eight-member board, headed by Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed, in the presence of a magistrate, victim’s family and lawyer and the investigating officer of the case performed the exhumation. The post-mortem examination continued for one hour and fifteen minutes and the body was buried again at around 1:33pm “We have collected samples for positive identification, chemical analysis and gunshot residue. The cause of death is kept reserved for laboratory reports,” Dr Syed told Dawn . Regarding autopsy, she said that multiple injuries were found on the head and face. “Fractured rib on the back which is the entry wound of the gunshot [that] exit from front,” she said. She said the body bore “injuries in right flank and feet [and] congealed black substance present in mouth and throat”. Lawyer demands new investigation team Later in the evening, lawyer for Raza’s family Advocate Jibran Nasir alleged that the 25-year-old had been tortured before being murdered and demanded that the entire investigation team be replaced. Speaking to the media, he said the medical report of the second post-mortem detailed some of the alleged injuries Raza had sustained before his death. “This was murder following torture — the murder of a happy, ambitious and educated young man from Karachi,” he alleged. The lawyer said that Raza had wounds to his forehead and a fractured nose, as well as swelling and congealed blood around his lower jaw, consistent with having been punched. “There is a fracture to his temple above his ear, indicating he was struck,” he alleged. “In the tongue area, a congealed black substance was discovered, which is not naturally found in the body. This substance has been taken and sent to a lab to see what he was forced to ingest,” he said. “Now we come to the firearm injury, where it was earlier said that he was shot in the chest and the bullet exited through his back. We have now proven 110 per cent that the bullet entered his back and exited after breaking and fracturing his ribs,” he said, referring to the fresh autopsy. The family’s lawyer also criticised senior police officials, alleging that they “do not want to investigate, but rather humiliate, above his ear, indicating he was struck,” he alleged. “In the tongue area, a congealed black substance was discovered, which is not naturally found in the body. This substance has been taken and sent to a lab to see what he was forced to ingest,” he said. “Now we come to the firearm injury, where it was earlier said that he was shot in the chest and the bullet exited through his back. We have now proven 110 per cent that the bullet entered his back and exited after breaking and fracturing his ribs,” he said, referring to the fresh autopsy. The family’s lawyer also criticised senior police officials, alleging that they “do not want to investigate, but rather humiliate, harass and exhaust the family”. “They are finding months-old recordings and frustrating, emotionally exhausting and humiliating Mir Hussain and Maryam Hussain. Are you investigating or harassing them? They sat them in their offices and told them repeatedly, ‘It’s a suicide, accept it’,” the advocate claimed further. Advocate Nasir added that he and the family had “no faith” in the investigation team and that they wanted the entire team changed. Raza’s father, Mir Hussain, told reporters that he had maintained since July 30 that his son’s death was a brutal murder. “We saw the body and told them [that it was murder], but they kept saying, ‘Suicide, suicide, suicide,’” he said. Mir Hussain said it “brought us peace” to learn that their claims that Raza had been attacked before his death were true. “We have said it was murder from the start,” he added. “Why are they hiding the killers?” Published in Dawn, August 9th, 2026

items.title: Court sentences barber for dumping refuse in public drain
items.description: A Hohoe Magistrate Court has sentenced Ekpane Seyram, a barber for collecting and dumping rubbish into a public drain. Ekpane pleaded guilty to the charge and was sentenced on his own plea to a fine of GHS 600 or would serve two months in prison in default. Mr Daniel Dotse Eklo, Environmental Health Analyst, Prosecuting, told the court, presided over by the relieving judge, Mr Lambert Y. Keriba, that the convict on Monday July 27, at about 2000 hours was caught dumping rubbish into the public drain around the Konuvie Plaza area. He said the activity of the convict was captured on a video and subsequently shared on Facebook. Mr Eklo said the incident caught the attention of the Municipal Chief Executive (MCE) and the Environmental Health Office at about 2126 hours the same day. He said the Environmental Health Unit in collaboration with the MCE through an investigation got the convict on Wednesday at about 1030 hours who accepted liability to the offence upon interrogation. Mr Eklo said the convict added that he collected the rubbish in and around a drinking bar where he had been staying belonging to one Madam Cecilia Attamah and Vincentia Attamah around the Konuvie area and dumped the same in the public drain around the area. He said the Assembly placed skip containers at vantage points in the Municipality for the collection and proper disposal of refuse. He said: “The Konuvie area is behind the Total Fuel Station around the station traffic light which is just about 150 meters from the Low Cost down and Market area container site.” He described the convict’s action as barbaric and inimical to the environment which could lead to flooding and outbreak of diseases.

items.title: Ban: to what end?
items.description: IN April I was living in Islamabad, in a leafy neighbourhood I had moved to after a few months cooped up in the Red Zone. The talks were on and the city was full of foreign correspondents. We passed a coffee shop on our way out of town and half the café was press. What I remember is how much everybody loved Islamabad. On camera and off it. The hills, the food, the hospitality. Testimonials. The state was delighted, and none of it required a form. It is August now. Those same correspondents cannot travel to any city outside Islamabad, Lahore and Karachi to produce a story without a No Objection Certificate from the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The fixers who drove them around must register on a government portal, as must freelancers, translators and camera operators. For a weekend in Murree, a journalist may apply. Permission may be granted within three working days. Feted in April. Registered in August. We do not even change the cast. And Al Jazeera ’s website has not opened from my desk in Karachi since last Sunday. Two browsers, a phone on mobile data. The page sits there and gives up. No order has been published. The PTA has confirmed nothing. What the ministry did say was that it had taken note of Al Jazeera ’s “selective reporting”, that the channel had sought to “misrepresent” the elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and that such “yellow journalism” confirmed the agenda of external actors with vested interests. A government may say that. It should contest any report it dislikes, and it has every means to do so. Restricting access to the report is the thing nobody has put in writing. That distinction matters more than it sounds. A rebuttal adds to the record. A block subtracts from it, and what it subtracts is not the story. It is the ability to check the story. What exactly did the Al Jazeera ban achieve? Because the appetite does not disappear when the reporting does. Nobody stops wanting to know. They simply take what is left, and what is left is whatever costs nothing to produce. Reporting from a difficult district costs money, time, risk and now paperwork. A monologue about that district, filmed in a bedroom in Lahore or London, costs nothing and is regulated by nobody. Every restriction we impose falls on the expensive, checkable kind of journalism and leaves the cheap, unverifiable kind entirely untouched. Then, when a figure appears that the state does not like, it has no way to disprove it. It has spent years dismantling the means by which anything could be disproved. The number stands, uncheckable, and the denial is worth exactly as much as the claim. So, what does a ban achieve? YouTube was blocked in September 2012 for three years. The film that caused it was never removed from the internet. Anyone determined used a proxy. Parliament passed a unanimous resolution asking for it to end. It lifted only because Google agreed to launch a local version. X was blocked in February 2024 after being used to raise allegations of election fraud. It returned 15 months later. VPN use is estimated to have risen 6,000 per cent, and Pakistan recorded the highest financial losses in the world from internet restrictions that year. Cabinet ministers used VPNs to reach the platform their own government had blocked. Al Jazeera was blocked once before, in 2013, after publishing the Abbottabad Commission report. The report was read worldwide. None achieved what the ban was for. Each one ended, but not one because it ‘worked’. What survived each was the impression that the state had something to hide, the one outcome a ban cannot reverse. We are told each time that this is an exception. A parti­cular provocation, a particular mom­ent. The Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines, 2026, remove that alibi. They are not a response to anything. They are the permanent version. On Wednesday, the BBC said it was “extremely concerned” and called for the restrictions to be reversed. Its statement noted that it reaches around 8.6 million people in Pakistan every week, and that its journalists, including local staff here, must be able to travel the country to hear the voices of ordinary citizens. This is what the ban achieved. Not less scrutiny. A BBC statement, a joint appeal from local and international rights groups, and a week of coverage abroad about Pakistan restricting the press. The ministry warned of external actors with vested interests. Then it went and produced them. A confident state does not need to clear the room before it makes its case. It makes the case. So, who will be left to say what happened. And when nobody is, whose account will we be arguing about next? The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi. X: @ LedeingLady Published in Dawn, August 9th, 2026

items.title: Six days to Osun election: 18 ‘killed’ as fears of more violence mount
items.description: •Osogbo, Ede, Ife, Oriade, Ijebu-Ijesha, Ilobu, Ikire emerge as flashpoints •Deployment of 15,000 policemen divides stakeholders By Shina Abubakar Fresh fears of further violence have gripped Osun State ahead of the August 15 governorship election, with the two major opposition parties, the All Progressives Congress, APC, and Accord Party, claiming to have lost a combined 18 members in the build-up to the poll. . The development has heightened concerns over the safety of voters, political parties and election officials as the state prepares for the governorship election, with the deployment of 15,000 policemen generating divergent reactions among political parties and civil society organisations. Specifically, the build-up to the August 15 election has been punctuated by a series of violent incidents across the state, ranging from attacks on party supporters and campaign convoys to shootings and alleged assassination attempts. Gunmen In May, an Accord Party member, Kolade Eluyera, was killed in Irewole Local Government Area, an incident the party attributed to alleged APC supporters, a claim rejected by the opposition party. The violence escalated on June 3 when the Accord chairman in Osogbo Local Government, Asimiyu Ajibola, was shot by gunmen and left receiving treatment in hospital. Expectedly, the incident further heightened tension between the rival camps. There was another reported death in Esa-Oke, where an Accord supporter, Ajayi Rogba, was killed during the period of heightened political activities. The incident again triggered accusations, with Accord supporters linking the killing to political violence, while APC members in the area denied involvement and warned against politicising the incident. Earlier, campaign activities in Ede, Osogbo and other parts of the state had also been disrupted by clashes, shootings and attacks on campaign convoys, reinforcing concerns that political disagreements were increasingly taking a violent dimension. The scale of the violence has since become a major concern ahead of next week’s poll. 13 fatalities For example, Kimpact Development Initiative said 44 election-related violent incidents resulting in 13 fatalities were recorded in Osun between October 2025 and June 2026. However, the political parties in separate chats with Sunday Vanguard, presented higher figures in relation to their members’ deaths. While the APC campaign council alleged that 10 of its members had been killed during the electioneering period, the Accord Party said eight of its people had also lost their lives. The parties have continued to trade accusations over responsibility for the violence, with each accusing the other of being behind attacks on its members. Although the combined figure of 18 deaths claimed by the two parties has not been independently established as a single death toll, the allegations have heightened fears of possible reprisal attacks and further violence before, during and after the election. The security situation has therefore become a major issue in the final days of the campaign, with stakeholders divided over whether the deployment of 15,000 policemen would help prevent violence or amount to militarisation of the electoral process. 10 of our members ‘ve been killed — APC Campaign Council The APC campaign council said the number of personnel deployed was less important than the professionalism, equipment and capacity of security agencies to ensure a free, fair and credible election. A member of the APC campaign council, Mr Kehinde Ayantunji, who spoke on behalf of the chairman, said the 15,000 personnel could be meaningless if they lacked the proper equipment and training needed to ensure a peaceful poll. Ayantunji said: “Since the beginning of this campaign, they have killed nothing less than 10 members of our party in Ilesa, Iwo, Osogbo, Ijebu-Jesa and some other communities. It is unfortunate that human life is involved and there is no election that is worth the life of any human being.” Speaking on the deployment of police officers, he said the party was not interested in the number of personnel but in the conduct of a free and fair election. He said: “Most important thing is not about number, it’s about the professional conduct of the Police, capacity to protect the people’s vote, we are interested in free, fair and credible election, we are also interested in adequate security to ensure that the Accord members do not succeed in creating fear and apprehension in the mind of the people so that our supporters and party members can come out to vote for the candidate of their choice.” The police, he said, “must do everything possible in terms of personnel, equipment, strategy and logistics to make sure that every vote counts in all the 3,761 polling units we have in Osun State. That’s our stand.” Oriade, Ijebu-Ijesha, Ikire On its part, the Accord Party said the number of policemen deployed might not be adequate considering the level of violence witnessed in some towns across the state, even as it called for more security personnel to ensure the safety of voters and votes. The party’s Media Director, Mr Oladele Bamiji, said: “The Accord party has lost about eight people to violence since since the commencement of this campaign. We have seen killings in Oriade, Ijebu-Jesha, Ilobu, Ikire to be precise and even in Osogbo. “The level of violence has been so bad, because people who have humanity at heart, who have blood running in their vein cannot be happy to loose just single person not to talk of eight. So, it is disheartening, frightening at the same time. People descend so low just because of electioneering, it is not a good way to lead people and it is a very bad moment for everyone.” Bamiji also questioned the numerical arrangement of the deployment, considering the number of polling units across the state. “I still don’t know the mathematical arrangement, we have very close to 4000 polling units in Osun State and we have four or five officers per polling units. To me, it is not so big, it is even inadequate. If a smaller state in terms of Local government like Ekiti, have more than us, I think there should be even more deployment. We understand that the Police are not the only security required for the electioneering, other security operatives will be around. I want to believe that they will compliment each other and have a peaceful election,” he said. It’s militarisation of election, says Osun Masterminds However, a coalition of civil society organisations in the state, The Osun Masterminds, expressed worry that the heavy deployment amounted to militarisation of the polls. The spokesperson for the group, Mr Ayo Ologunde, said: “The deployment of 15,000 Police men for gubernatorial election in Osun signifies militarisation, the State and the Nation as a whole should have grown to a level where election should not be seen as war, even in a situation of war, 15,000 police officers is a lot. “Police uniform create fear in the mind of the citizens, which causes voters apathy, now that 15,000 police have been deployed, some of them will start illegal checkpoint across the local government they are taken to, people won’t be able to walk freely at night for the fear of checkpoint in a state where there should be freedom of movement. “Second, you have created likely security loop holes in the other states, because criminals are not resting, they know that on the day of election, there will be less policemen in the neighbouring state, hoodlums will want to take advantage of that deployment to commit crime in neighbouring state.” In addition, he said: “Voting is a process of electing leaders, not a process of militarisation or to create undue fear. “These policemen are not going to be deployed for free, they will be given allowances. Instead of giving them millions of naira as election allowance. Why don’t you use the money for infrastructure. It is a waste of resources at a time like this in the nation?” 15,000 policemen will stop violence — Dialogue 365 However, the Convener of Dialogue 365, Mr Saka Waheed, backed the deployment, saying it was necessary to stop the violence and allow the conduct of a peaceful election. Waheed said: “We demanded for protection, now we are having it. We cannot call it militarisation, the incessant killing in the past months show that if there is no enough security, there may be further killings on election day; it will be very unfortunate to allow miscreants take over our electoral process killing people.” He added: “Let us have more than that, as long as our people will be secured that’s being proactive there can even be up to 50,000. We have an history of security deployment in Osun, even when those security came to harass our people during the Aregbesola time, despite that people still came out to say this is who we want as our Governor.” Heavy deployment of security personnel driven by intelligence—ex-lawmaker A former chairman of the House of Assembly Committee on Information, Mr Olatunbosun Oyintiloye, also threw his weight behind the deployment, saying it may be driven by intelligence available to the Federal Government. Oyintiloye said: “The country faces security challenges, and the heavy deployment of security personnel to Osun State may be driven by intelligence available to the Federal Government. “Such deployments are routine during election periods, and the state is familiar with them. There is, therefore, no cause for alarm. “Nonetheless, concerns over rising incidents of extrajudicial killings remain. Security agencies must act decisively, while the government ramps up public sensitisation to encourage voter turnout without fear.” With the election only days away, attention has consequently shifted to how the security agencies will manage the volatile political environment, particularly in areas considered flashpoints. The competing claims by APC and Accord over the deaths of their members have also raised fresh concerns about possible retaliation and the potential for political violence to escalate before, during and after the election. Stakeholders have therefore called for restraint among political parties and their supporters, while urging security agencies to ensure that the heavy deployment is used to protect voters and maintain peace rather than intimidate the electorate. items.title: Counterterrorism paradox
items.description: PAKISTAN’S security forces are fighting terrorism with commitment and high intensity. From sanitisation campaigns and intelligence-based operations to targeted raids and large-scale engagements, the tempo of action is rising. Yet terrorist violence is not receding. July recorded the year’s highest number of attacks , underscoring the grim reality that the security situation is deteriorating, particularly in KP and Balochistan, despite mounting operational pressure on terrorist groups. The return of violence to areas once declared cleared of terrorism is especially troubling. Last week, Swat suffered a devastating suicide bombing outside the Kabal police station. The attacker struck as participants were leaving the Swat People’s Peace Uprising, organised by residents and civil society groups alarmed by renewed terrorist activity in the valley. Seventeen people, including police personnel and civilians, were killed, while more than a dozen were wounded. Though there is confusion about whether the TTP had targeted the peace rally or the police station, whatever the group’s intentions, the attack raises a significant question about how and why the terrorists are increasing their operational base. Balochistan, meanwhile, experienced one of its worst months of violence in recent years. July saw coordinated, high-impact attacks across Mastung, Lasbela, Ziarat, Kech and Khuzdar. These incidents demonstrated both the geographic reach of armed terrorist groups and their ability to challenge the state simultaneously in dispersed locations. The security response was substantial. According to data maintained by the Pak Institute for Peace Studies, 26 anti-militant operations were recorded across Pakistan in July, compared with 24 in June. Conducted mainly by the army, Frontier Corps and police counterterrorism departments, these operations killed 205 terrorists. Eighteen operations took place in Balochistan and eight in KP. In Quetta and the adjoining Shaban and Hanna Urak areas alone, six operations reportedly killed 68 militants. The country lacks a coordinated strategy that converts operational success into durable peace. These figures reveal both capability and imbalance. Only five suspected terrorists were arrested during the month, all in Karachi. They were allegedly affiliated with the banned Balochistan Liberation Army, Jamaatul Ahrar and Lashkar-i-Jhangvi. The overwhelming ratio of deaths to arrests suggests an increasing reliance on lethal force and a weakness in the investigative, prosecutorial and intelligence-gathering dimensions of counterterrorism. Arrests can expose facilitators, financiers, recruiters and communication networks; dead militants rarely do. Meanwhile, human rights groups continue to express concern over enforced disappearances, deepening mistrust in already alienated communities. In KP, the threat remains centred on the banned TTP and allied factions, including the Hafiz Gul Bahadur group. Since violence resurged in 2021, attacks have been concentrated largely in the southern districts and former tribal areas. Since early 2026, however, the operational map has widened. Militants are increasingly testing settled districts and extending networks towards Balo­chistan and potentially southern Punjab. Their continued mobility and logistical reach, despite sustained operations, show that they retain recruitment, facilitation and support structures. Their tactics are also evolving. Suicide bombings, targeted killings and assaults on police and military installations remain central, but militants are increasingly experimenting with quadcopters and drones for explosive attacks. Government officials, civilians and public infrastructure are also being targeted. The objective is broader than producing casualties: it is to erode state authority, frighten communities and disrupt everyday governance. Public anger over counterterrorism methods adds another layer of risk. The residents of Hassankhel recently protested outside the Peshawar Press Club against alleged drone strikes in their area. They claimed that civilians, including women and children, had been killed and that schools, mosques and roads had been damaged. Whether or not each allegation is established, such protests must be investigated transparently. Civilian harm, or even the perception that it is being ignored, provides militants with propaganda and weakens cooperation between communities and the state. The regional dimension further complicates the challenge. Islamabad’s attempts to pursue Kabul on the TTP sanctuaries inside Afghanistan have not yielded results, and cross-border networks remain a major internal security concern. Still, escalating hostility with Afghanistan cannot substitute for a coherent domestic strategy. Border pressure may constrain the terrorists; it cannot repair governance deficits, police weaknesses or local alienation. Recent counterterrorism operations in Bannu, Quetta and elsewhere confirm considerable operational capacity; however, whether these are translating into long-term success is not clear. The harder question is whether or not tactical successes are producing strategic stability. The evidence suggests they are not. Sanitising an area is not the same as securing it; killing militants is not the same as dismantling the ecosystem that sustains militancy. In a similar context, Balochistan presents an even more complex landscape. Violent Baloch organisations operate alongside religiously inspi­red terrorist groups such as the TTP and IS-K. The province’s vast territory, difficult terrain and thin administrative presence allow militants to disrupt roads, movement and economic activity before security forces can respond. But geography explains only part of the problem. Political exclusion, socioeconomic deprivation, weak public services and a distrust of state institutions create openings that terrorists exploit, particularly among frustrated youth. Saner voices among politicians and intellectuals have long advised that a political solution must be given a full chance and should not be abandoned along the way. Civilian governance must occupy the space rec­overed by security forces. Functional local ad­­min­istrations, reliable services, political engagement and employment opportunities can deny terroris­ts the grievances they weaponise. Commu­ni­ties shou­­ld be treated as partners, not merely as populations to be controlled; their knowledge can strengthen early warning and prevent infiltration. Pakistan’s problem, therefore, is not a shortage of operations. It is the absence of a coordinated strategy that converts operational successes into durable peace. Without accountable governance, political inclusion, capable policing, regional diplomacy and community trust, the state will keep clearing the same ground, and terrorists will keep returning to it. The stakes are now dangerously high nationwide. The writer is a security analyst. Published in Dawn, August 9th, 2026
