items.title: Iran issues demands for reopening of Hormuz
items.description: Iran set preconditions on Saturday for a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, including compensation for war damages, complicating a potential deal to open the waterway essential to the world economy. Tehran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait since the United States and Israel struck Iran in late February, and wants to charge tolls for passage, attacking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route.

items.title: Vers un monde à +2 °C ? Les 30 données de l’été du basculement écologique
items.description: Nous ne sommes qu’à la moitié de l’été, mais les données déjà disponibles indiquent un moment de bascule. Le changement climatique est désormais une réalité tangible, se manifestant par une série de records simultanés dans les domaines atmosphérique, océanique, sanitaire et économique. Nous avons compilé trente données afin de nous situer dans cette trajectoire. Juin 2026 a été un mois hors norme : il s'agit du mois le plus chaud jamais enregistré en Europe occidentale et du deuxième au niveau mondial, selon Copernicus Record heatwave brings hottest June for western Europe during second-warmest June globally », Copernicus, 9 juillet 2026.'> 1 . Jamais un mois de juin n'avait été aussi chaud en Europe occidentale : 20,74 °C de moyenne, soit 3,06 °C au-dessus de la normale 1991-2020. Le précédent record datait de juin 2025. Au niveau mondial, la température moyenne en juin a été supérieure de 1,39 °C aux niveaux préindustriels. La canicule de la fin du mois de juin a fait bondir le thermomètre de 14 à 18 °C au-dessus des normales en Europe centrale, battant des records mensuels et absolus dans plusieurs pays, dont l'Allemagne et la République tchèque. L’Allemagne a battu son record national absolu de température, trois jours de suite, avec des records allant jusqu'à 41,7 °C le 28 juin à Coschen. Au Danemark, le record national absolu a été enregistré à 37 °C, tandis que le Royaume-Uni effaçait son record de juin trois jours consécutifs, jusqu'à 37,3 °C relevés le 26 juin à Santon Downham (Suffolk), loin devant l'ancien record de 35,6 °C qui tenait depuis 1976. Le mercredi 24 juin, il faisait plus chaud en France que dans près d’un tiers du désert du Sahara . Aussi chaud à Paris (41°C) qu'à Abou Dhabi, aux Émirats arabes unis, à Strasbourg (37 °C) qu'à Niamey au Niger, à Brest (36 °C) qu'à Tombouctou au Mali, et à Bordeaux (42 °C) qu'à Riyad en Arabie saoudite. Avec 40,7 °C Barcelone a enregistré la température la plus élevée de ses 112 années de relevés le 8 juillet. Ailleurs dans le monde, selon les données de la NOAA, la capitale japonaise affiche en juillet-août des températures et une humidité proches de celles de Bangkok et de Singapour. A Pékin, le volume annuel de précipitations a augmenté de 20 % en dix ans. Le 27 avril, les 50 villes les plus chaudes de la planète se trouvaient toutes en Inde, avec une température maximale moyenne de 44,7 °C. À Colombo, au Sri Lanka, l'écart entre l'indice de chaleur de 46 °C et la température de 32 °C au thermomètre tient à un taux d'humidité de 84 %. Un air proche de la saturation n'absorbe plus la transpiration et le corps se retrouve alors sans moyen d'évacuer sa chaleur. En Europe, qui se réchauffe deux fois plus vite que la moyenne mondiale, la chaleur a un effet net sur la mortalité. Selon Santé publique France, 5 764 décès en excès ont été recensés, toutes causes confondues, lors de l'épisode de canicule qui a touché la France du 17 juin au 2 juillet 5 764 décès en excès en France durant la période de canicule du 17 juin au 2 juillet », Santé publique France, juillet 2026.'> 2 . La surmortalité liée à la chaleur, enregistrée en quelques semaines seulement cet été, se situe, elle, à près de 10 000 morts, selon l’OMS — un bilan encore partiel, établi sur la base des données de cinq pays seulement. La mortalité liée à la chaleur en Europe a augmenté de 30 % en vingt ans, causant plus de 200 000 décès au cours des quatre dernières années. Les températures dans les océans sont en nette augmentation. En juin, la température moyenne de surface des océans libres de glace a atteint un niveau jamais mesuré pour un mois de juin : 21,0 °C, soit plus que les records de 2023 et 2024 June 2026 : Global Ocean Temperatures Reach New Record », Copernicus Marine Service, juillet 2026.'> 3 . 82 % de l’océan mondial était en situation de canicule marine fin juin, la deuxième plus grande étendue jamais observée. L’anomalie moyenne enregistrée en juin en Méditerranée nord-occidentale, touchée par une canicule marine record se situe à +5,2 °C. Fin juillet, plus de 435 000 hectares avaient brûlé à l’échelle de l’Union Seasonal Trend — EU27 », Système européen d’information sur les feux de forêt (EFFIS), Copernicus Emergency Management Service, données consultées le 3 août 2026.'> 4 et ce chiffre dépasse les 500 000 début août. L’Espagne concentre à elle seule plus de 200 000 hectares brûlés, soit 0,4 % de son territoire. Nous ne sommes qu'au début du mois d'août mais il faut déjà regarder vers 2027 : pour la première fois, un mois pourrait y dépasser les +2 °C par rapport aux niveaux préindustriels. Selon les dernières projections de la Rosenstiel School de l'université de Miami, il y a 35 à 40 % de chances que la température mondiale moyenne dépasse pour la première fois les + 2 °C par rapport aux niveaux préindustriels, sur un mois donné, au début de l'année 2027. C'est ce que pourrait provoquer l'épisode El Niño de cette année, qui pourrait être parmi les plus puissants jamais enregistrés. En effet, ce phénomène amplifie mécaniquement la hausse des températures causée par la concentration de gaz à effet de serre. Les régions les plus exposées au réchauffement d'El Niño sont l'Amérique, l'Afrique et l'Australie — mais, contrairement aux épisodes précédents, l'Europe pourrait également être touchée, de cet automne jusqu'au printemps 2027. El Niño provoque des sécheresses en Inde, en Afrique australe et en Océanie, ainsi qu'un temps plus humide dans le sud de l'Amérique, dans le bassin du golfe du Mexique et dans la Corne de l'Afrique. Selon Copernicus, l’objectif de l’Accord de Paris de limiter la hausse des températures à 1,5 °C est pratiquement irréalisable au vu de la trajectoire actuelle — le franchissement durable du seuil est attendu d’ici environ quatre ans Record heatwave brings hottest June for western Europe during second-warmest June globally » Copernicus, 9 juillet 2026.'> 5 . Le basculement a déjà un coût économique mesurable. Selon le PIIE, El Niño pourrait causer des pertes de 700 à 3 100 milliards de dollars à l’économie mondiale au cours des cinq prochaines années. L’effet d’un réchauffement climatique de 2,2 °C d’ici 2050 pourrait entraîner une baisse de 10 à 20 % du PIB mondial, selon Oxford Economics, qui évoque, à + 5 °C d’ici 2100, une « annihilation économique ». La hausse des températures pourrait coûter à l’économie indienne jusqu’à 4,5 % de son PIB d’ici 2030 . La hausse des températures provoque également des perturbations d'ordre infrastructurel. Fin juillet, l’Autorité du canal de Panama a suspendu une partie de son système de réservation, car les sécheresses ont fait baisser le niveau des réservoirs qui alimentent la voie d’eau reliant l’océan Pacifique à l’océan Atlantique. Le Rhin, artère des industries chimiques, des raffineries et des aciéries européennes qui relie l’Allemagne, la Suisse et la France aux ports néerlandais, touche des niveaux proches de creux pluri-décennaux. Le Danube, le Pô, le Rhône et la Saône affichent également des débits très inférieurs aux moyennes . Le niveau historiquement bas du Danube a contraint la Roumanie et la Hongrie à exploiter leurs centrales nucléaires à capacité réduite, et à demander aux ménages comme aux entreprises de limiter leur consommation aux heures de pointe. Dacia et Ford ont suspendu leur production. La Roumanie a dû arrêter l'un des deux réacteurs de Cernavodă, qui fournit 20 % de son électricité ; le 3 août, sa marine a fait sauter 180 kg d'explosifs dans le lit du fleuve pour rediriger l'eau de refroidissement vers la centrale. La fin de la banane ? Sous les tropiques, les bananes Cavendish sont confrontées à un risque réel de disparition , en raison des conditions extrêmes, des maladies et des parasites favorisés par le changement climatique. L’article Vers un monde à +2 °C ? Les 30 données de l’été du basculement écologique est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Ibadan meeting: Atiku, Obi, Kwankwaso still have opportunity for grand alliance — Ologbondiyan
items.description: •2027: ‘Hungry Nigerians, not the opposition, will give Tinubu sleepless nights’ By Luminous Jannamike, Abuja Few opposition figures have witnessed Nigeria’s political twists and realignments from as close a vantage point as Kola Ologbondiyan. A former National Publicity Secretary of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), he now serves as Special Adviser on Media and Publicity to the National Chairman of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Senator David Mark, placing him at the centre of fresh efforts to forge a formidable opposition ahead of the 2027 general election. In this interview, Ologbondiyan speaks on the prospects of a united opposition, the PDP’s lingering crisis, the ADC’s mission, and why he believes President Bola Tinubu’s biggest political test in 2027 will come not from rival parties, but from millions of Nigerians battling economic hardship. Excerpts: Kola Ologbondiyan You spent years shaping the PDP’s public communication. Looking at where the opposition stands today, with the ADC and NDC pulling in different directions, do you still believe, it can mount a credible challenge to President Tinubu before the January 2027 election? I strongly believe so. And my belief is based on the decision reached at the meeting held in Ibadan among all the opposition political parties to look at that proposed grand alliance. The decision reached by the majority of the opposition parties was that, at the nick of time, they were going to pull together. I believe that the opposition political parties are going to realign and work in the direction of rescuing our nation from the path of perdition into which it is gradually drifting. When Peter Obi and Rabiu Kwankwaso left the ADC coalition in May, what really went wrong? Was it a clash of personalities or disagreement over zoning or were there deeper issues Nigerians still don’t know about? I think when the decision was taken to leave the ADC, my reading was that the decision was arrived at in a hurry. And I said this publicly because no point had been reached in the discussion to arrive at the position of leaving the alliance. And that is why I still believe that the opposition, if it can read the game properly, still has the opportunity for the grand alliance which the Ibadan meeting projected. So, you think there is no real danger that both Atiku Abubakar and Obi/Kwankwaso camps will split the opposition vote again, just as happened in 2023? What I’m saying, essentially, is that at the point at which the camps of Peter Obi as well as Kwankwaso left the coalition, no decision had been reached to warrant their departure. Because talks were still ongoing. I’ve also said that the best decision that can rescue our nation today is a government of national unity. And that this government of national unity was a disposition which the opposition political parties were working towards when they arrived at the Ibadan coalition’s decision, which is that all the political parties must come together, have one candidate, and work together. And I’m saying that I do not believe, I don’t want to say, that that decision has been foreclosed. I don’t want to say or hold on to the notion that that decision is dead. I believe that if the opposition political parties are determined to rescue this nation, the best approach is for all opposition political parties to pull together. The PDP has elected a new national leadership this year? In your assessment, does the party still have the reach and strength to compete nationally? Do you think the PDP has lost too much ground? I think my worry about the PDP is, I know you talked about the PDP today, but which PDP are you talking about? I think that is the challenge that I have. And I say so essentially because the role of the PDP was to serve as an opposition political party after losing power in 2015. But can we, with every sense of responsibility, say that the PDP as we have it now will serve that same purpose? I think the answer is no. And I want to leave it at that. Many Nigerians argue that opposition parties become vocal only when elections are around the corner. But after the elections, everybody seems to go back to their various cocoons. Why has the opposition struggled to sustain pressure on the government over the economy, insecurity and the cost-of-living crisis? I give it to the African Democratic Congress (ADC) coalition. Since it came onto the political scene about a year ago, I think the party spokesman Bolaji Abdullahi has been consistent in holding the government in power to its responsibilities. So I think that, moving forward, even if the party continues in that line, irrespective of what the disposition is after the 2027 election, I think it should emerge as a political party that has focus, that has determination, and that is going to serve the interests of Nigerians. Both the ADC and NDC are still facing legal disputes. How confident are you that neither party will run into serious legal obstacles allegedly put in their way by the ruling party before the next general election? I’m very confident, as long as the judiciary stands upright and continues to work in the interests of our democracy. Because if you look at the entirety of the matters in court, without being judgmental and without showing any form of disrespect to the judiciary, I think there are no issues. For instance, when you look at the issue of the party’s deregistration, and Nigerians are saying they are going to deregister it, I can say to you that I can’t see that happening because the law is very clear. I am not a lawyer; I never claimed to be one either. But it is clear what the law stipulates. It says that either you have won 25 per cent in the presidential election, or you have done this, or you have done that. The provisions of the law are not tied to one issue. You understand? And also, it is INEC that has the authority to decide which party to recognise or not recognise. So when you talk about deregistration and the whole issue, I don’t even look at the circumstances of everything that has happened. To me, the way I see it, it is just bringing the Presidency into disrepute because the law is very clear on how a party can be deregistered. You don’t just form a group suddenly, go to court suddenly, and then say that so-and-so party should not be registered. Then you have a Chief of Staff to the President, the face of the Presidency, who comes out and says that somebody (Hon. Leke Abejide) who left his party and took his party’s structure should go and scatter a particular political party. You just look at all this and discover that there is an arrangement to even bring the democracy that we all live for into disrepute and to a sudden death. Beyond criticising the APC, what is that one policy proposal you believe clearly distinguishes the opposition and gives Nigerians a genuine alternative? I think I would say that one distinguishing factor between the APC and the ADC coalition lies in the character of those who left the ruling party for the ADC. And I say so clearly because one thing that the ADC coalition has stood for since its inception, and also in the new turnaround of the political party, is the battle to ensure that democracy survives. I think that has been the focus. We object to a system that gives power to one man, to an individual, because democracy cannot thrive in a situation where only one man is respected and accorded the rights of a king in a democratic setting. So I think if you look at the ADC, that is the area of focus from the new turnaround of the political party. Proceeding from there, what differentiates the ADC from the APC? I will clearly tell you that the ADC has a vision of working with Nigerians to bring about a government that will work only in the interests of Nigerians, a government whose focus shall be to ensure that Nigerians thrive democratically and that the people benefit from democracy. Let’s go back a little to the Second Republic. When you mention the UPN in the Second Republic, what comes to mind is free education and an egalitarian society. When you mention the NPN, what comes to mind is agriculture, housing, and so on and so forth. When you mention the PRP, you think about the Talakawa. Come to the Fourth Republic. Mention any political party, any one, that gives you a clear picture of what it stands for. It is only the ADC now that can clearly say that it stands for democracy and is completely opposed to one-man rule. And I think that’s where we are. Apart from the prominent opposition leaders Atiku, Obi, and Kwankwaso, do you see any other emerging figures Nigerians should keep an eye on after the 2027 vote and ahead of 2031? I think what is common to the majority of Nigerians as we speak today is how to stop this government through the ballot. For it from proceeding beyond 2027. I think that is the task. And I would advise that the political groupings, whether in the PDP, the ADC, or wherever, the common denominator should be this: How do we rebuild this country? How do we rework this country using every democratic means to stop this suffering from continuing? I think that is the focus for now. I don’t want to go beyond that. The President recently declared that he was ready to “fight to finish”, politically. How should the opposition interpret that statement? Well, I believe that, for instance, the African Democratic Congress, where I belong, has already made its position very, very clear. But beyond that, I think there is a misconception in what Mr President said, and that misconception is on the part of Mr President. I think the President sees the issue of 2027 as one between him and the opposition political parties. The answer to that is no. I think the issue is between Mr President and Nigerians who are suffering, who are hungry, who have no money in their pockets. I think they are the people he should be prepared to contend with. And I am sure that, through their ballots, those Nigerians are also prepared to ensure that they vote against Mr President. So it is not about the opposition. It is a misconception to think or believe that the whole issue is between the President and the opposition political parties. Who are the people in the opposition political parties? They are Nigerians who do not want him to continue in office, and they are prepared, democratically, through their ballots, to stop him from continuing. If you had one minute to convince an undecided Nigerian voter that the opposition; not particularly the ADC, the PDP, or any specific party, will win in 2027, what would you say? Look, let me tell you. The facts speak for themselves. You don’t need to tell Nigerians anything. What are you going to tell them? That their lives are better today? The answer is no. What are you going to tell them? When the President came into office and said subsidy was gone and gone forever, those who believed him are now experiencing the consequences. There is no need to tell Nigerians anything. Nigerians are already telling themselves what they are passing through and what they are suffering. So, no, let’s not even go into that. The post Ibadan meeting: Atiku, Obi, Kwankwaso still have opportunity for grand alliance — Ologbondiyan appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Makkah agreement
items.description: IN the midst of a gruelling war between the US and Iran — currently at a stalemate — the signing of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on Friday is a highly symbolic development. It comes at a time when the American defence umbrella has proved of little help in protecting Saudi Arabia and the other Gulf Arab states. Rather, the presence of US military assets in these states has pulled them into the war, as the Iranians and their regional armed allies target these facilities. Seen in this context, many questions swirl around the new defence agreement, specifically the fact that it considers an attack against one signatory to be an attack against all. The prime minister, the Saudi crown prince and the Turkish president were all upbeat about the new pact. PM Shehbaz Sharif termed it “historic”, while President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said it is open to “friendly nations”. This is not an ‘Islamic Nato’. Moreover, similar alliances have been attempted before, such as the Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition founded in 2015 and headed by former army chief Gen Raheel Sharif. The latter alliance is not linked to any major operations. Pakistani-Saudi defence collaboration goes back decades, and the current pact only solidifies the arrangement, while also bringing Turkiye on board. But the question in many minds is what role the pact will play vis-à-vis Iran. A Saudi deputy minister has said the agreement “does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc”. This clarification is welcome. On the other hand, an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader has said that more cooperation among regional states “can secure its security”. If the US-Iran war remains unresolved and major hostilities erupt again, the new alliance will be put to the test, especially if Tehran resumes attacks on the pro-America GCC states. Suffice it to say, such alliances should work to reduce tensions between Muslims states, and not be used against any Muslim country. The US has shown it is uninterested in protecting its Gulf allies, even though the latter have purchased billions of dollars’ worth of weaponry from it. Instead of depending on the US or other foreign powers for security, regional states — indeed all OIC members — should pledge to refrain from aggression against each other. Iran should stop attacking the GCC states, while the Gulf sheikhdoms should stop foreign forces from using their soil against Iran. The Arabs and the Iranians cannot change their geography; they have to live side by side; hence it would be best if they worked out a modus vivendi for mutual security. Hopefully, the new defence agreement can promote unity within the Muslim world, instead of adding to the existing fissures. Published in Dawn, August 9th, 2026

items.title: Nigeria’s mass wedding – and how telling lovers from fraudsters is proving tricky
items.description: Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass wedding. For days the city’s streets have been buzzing with bridal parties and their families preparing outfits and attending other organised events. On Friday, brides in red hijabs with grooms in matching red hats and white robes went the palace of the Emir, the city’s traditional Muslim leader, for the main ceremony where they officially became husband and wife. The nuptials culminated on Saturday with a wedding breakfast hosted by Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, who offered his blessing to the newlyweds. The Kano state government sponsored this initiative, spending 1.5bn naira ($1m; £815,000) to support those tying the knot – providing the bride’s dowry and furniture for the couple’s first home. The scheme targets low-income individuals who cannot afford the significant financial costs associated with marriage. The annual event was initiated in 2012 by the then-governor when 100 couples – primarily widows and divorcees – wed at the palace. The mass weddings have continued under subsequent governors, with numbers expanding each year as demand has grown and included those in polygamous Muslim marriages. Such is the popularity of the scheme that 5,000 couples applied this year. The event is always overseen by the Hisbah – the city’s Islamic police force – and one of their main tasks is to vet the couples wanting to wed. Kano has a majority Muslim population and Sharia operates in the state alongside the secular legal system. Mujahid Aminudeen, deputy commander-general of the Hisbah, admits it is not an easy task. “Whenever we find out that there’s something dubious or fishy about a couple, we disqualify them,” he tells the BBC. He says some couples will go to great lengths to convince the authorities that they are a genuine love match when their eye is more on the benefits on offer. The Hisbah office has been very busy for weeks as brides and grooms try to ensure they made the final list The state government has spent approximately 1m naira ($735; £544) on each participating couple. According to the Hisbah, the support package a couple receives includes essential household items needed to establish a new home: beds, mattresses, bedsheets, pillows, furniture and food supplies. Each bride receives a dowry of 100,000 naira, while a further 100,000 naira is provided as start-up capital to encourage small-scale entrepreneurship and help the couple achieve financial self-reliance after marriage. All intending couples must undergo comprehensive medical examinations – including tests for HIV, hepatitis, pregnancy and genotype compatibility – before being cleared for the programme. Aminudeen revealed that some couples had been disqualified after being discovered to have altered their medical test results. In one case, an intending bride was found to have presented her brother as the groom in an attempt to benefit from the scheme. Local journalist Yusuf Ali Abdallah, who has covered the mass weddings for years, said Nigeria’s struggling economy had been fuelling desperation among the applicants this year. “As we all know, marriage involves spending money and the country’s economy is not bright at the moment,” he told the BBC. “This makes some people desperate to get on this list.” One couple who were already married had even attempted to present themselves as an intending pair before being detected and removed from the programme, he said. Other charlatans have tried to take advantage of those desperate to get on the sponsored list, which was made public two weeks ago. One Kano resident, who asked to be anonymous, said he had been asked to pay a bribe to get on the list. “But to be fair to the organisers, I later found out those who asked me for money were not Hisbah staff,” he said. He and his fiancée failed to be chosen for this August’s wedding but he said he would try again next year. Amina Alhassan, 24, says she could not have afforded to get married at the moment had it not been for the mass wedding scheme Aminudeen admitted that the Islamic police were aware of such allegations: “We have found that there are some people asking others to pay certain money so they can make the list.” But the Hisbah officer wanted to assure all those wishing to wed in future that the entire process should not cost them a single naira. “We want to announce to the people of Kano that the whole process is free: from the selection to the medicals and the goods set aside for couples – all are covered by the government.” One of successful grooms, 43-year-old clothes trader Rabiu Yusuf, agreed the process of applying to be married had gone smoothly for him. “Personally, no-one asked me for anything. I was told the government would sponsor it all,” he told the BBC. His new wife is Aisha Auwal – the couple met as she regularly visited his shop to buy clothes. Yusuf, who already has five children with his first wife, said he was “very happy and can’t wait to start a new life” with his customer-turned-bride. Twenty-four-year-old Amina Alhassan echoed his sentiments, adding that she had not encountered any problems when applying to marry 40-year-old Nura Abdullahi. Their union was first arranged by their families in Dambatta village before they presented themselves to the Hisbah. “Everything has been free and I want to commend the Kano government for this scheme because without it, many couldn’t have afforded to marry due to the high cost of living.” After Saturday’s wedding feast, the presentation of the household goods began. But it will take several more days for the excitement to die down in Kano and as the newlyweds busy themselves with setting up home together.

items.title: Insecurity: Scores of schools in 40 LGAs shut down
items.description: •Three states worst hit as non-state actors disrupt learning •Experts warn closures worsening out-of-school crisis, child labour, early marriage, radicalization By Nnamdi Ojiego, Musa Ubandawaki, Umar Yusuf, Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo, Peter Duru, Ndahi Marama, Golok Nanmwa, Haruna Aliyu, Yauziyya Lawal & Maryam Usman At least 65 secondary and primary schools have been shut or rendered non-functional by insecurity across northern Nigeria, findings by Sunday Vanguard have shown, with the closures cutting across dozens of local government areas and leaving thousands of children without normal access to classroom education. Affected schools are spread across Sokoto, Benue, Plateau, Borno, Kaduna and Kebbi, while insecurity has also disrupted academic activities in parts of Katsina, Adamawa and other northern states. The closures have been triggered by terrorist and bandit attacks, abductions, displacement of communities and fears of further attacks on pupils, students and teachers. In some communities, schools have remained shut for prolonged periods. In others, authorities have merged affected schools with institutions in safer locations or moved students to alternative centres to keep them in school. The development has raised fresh concerns over Nigeria’s already severe out-of-school crisis and the long-term consequences of keeping children away from classrooms. It has also persisted despite years of government and donor-backed interventions aimed at protecting schools from attacks, including the Safe Schools Initiative launched in 2014 after the abduction of 276 schoolgirls from Government Girls Secondary School, Chibok, Borno State. The initiative was established as a partnership involving the Federal Government, the United Nations and the private sector to protect schools in high-risk communities and ensure that children could continue their education despite insecurity. More than $30 million has been mobilised for the Safe Schools Initiative since its establishment, according to the Global Business Coalition for Education. The Federal Government later introduced the National Plan on Financing Safe Schools for 2023 to 2026, with a projected investment of ¦ 144.86 billion. The plan envisaged ¦ 32.58 billion in 2023, ¦ 36.98 billion in 2024, ¦ 37.15 billion in 2025 and ¦ 38.03 billion in 2026. Yet, more than a decade after the Safe Schools Initiative was launched, attacks continue to drive children away from schools. Sokoto shuts schools in 20 LGAs Sokoto State has recorded one of the most extensive current disruptions. Schools in 20 of the state’s 23 local government areas have been shut following security concerns, according to the state government. The Commissioner for Basic and Secondary Education, Prof Ahmad Ladan Ala, said the closure followed a directive from the Federal Government. He said schools across the state, including primary schools, had been closed indefinitely, with schools within Sokoto North, Sokoto South and Wamakko exempted. The President of the All Nigerian Conference of Principals of Secondary Schools, Muhammad Ikililu, said insecurity had also disrupted boarding education in the state for several years. According to him, boarding schools were moved to the state capital during the administration of former Governor Aminu Tambuwal because of insecurity in the North-West and Sokoto State in particular. He said some of the affected schools remained closed. Sunday Vanguard identified 14 schools affected by the current security situation across the state. They include Government Secondary School, Tureta; Government Secondary School, Tangaza; Government Girls Secondary School, Bodinga; Government Girls Secondary School, Tambuwal; Government Technical College, Goronyo; Government Secondary School, Gudu; Government Secondary School, Gwadabawa; Government Girls Secondary School, Illela; Government Secondary School, Yabo; Government Girls Secondary School, Rabah; Government Technical College, Binji; Government Secondary School, Kebbe; Government Secondary School, Dange; and Government Secondary School, Shagari. The governorship candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) in the state, Manir Muhammad Dan’iya, described the situation as a major setback to education and human capital development, saying the closures had deprived thousands of children of access to education. Benue In Benue, insecurity has forced the closure of numerous primary schools across Kwande, Gwer West, Guma and Logo local government areas. Repeated attacks and displacement have made several communities unsafe for teaching and learning, forcing schools to close and families to move to safer locations. Sunday Vanguard identified 35 affected schools in the state. They include LGEA NKST Science Primary School, Anyiin; LGEA RCM Primary School, Anyiin; LGEA Primary School, Anyiin; LGEA RCM Primary School, Igbur; LGEA Primary School, Chembe; LGEA Primary School, Iorza; LGEA NKST Primary School, Abeda-Shitile; LGEA RCM Primary School, Abeda-Shitile; LGEA RCM Primary School, Mchia; Shisho Unity Nursery and Primary School, Mchia; LGEA Primary School, Jootar; LGEA Primary School, Abiem; LGEA Primary School, Tyôgbihi; NKST Primary School, Azege; LGEA Primary School, Uzer; and RCM Primary School, Ikyule. Others are NKST Primary School, Mbakighir; NKST Primary School, Kurungu; NKST Primary School, Audu; NKST Primary School, Annakaa; LGEA Primary School, Abur-Kpera; NKST Primary School, Anungwa; NKST Primary School, Gwatse; LGEA Primary School, Aman; LGEA Primary School, Gbeleve; LGEA Primary School, Ugwe; RCM Primary School, Poovule; RCM Primary School, Ibôr; LGEA Primary School, Kwagh; LGEA Primary School, Vir; LGEA RCM Primary School, Akombo; LGEA Primary School, Ubver; LGEA Primary School, Ageraga; LGEA RCM Primary School, Shausu; and LGEA Primary School, Mou. Residents said the prolonged closure of schools had denied many children access to education. Some pupils have moved to safer communities to continue their studies, while others have dropped out completely following the displacement of their families. Borno In Borno, renewed attacks have again disrupted schooling in Askira-Uba Local Government Area. Sunday Vanguard’s correspondent identified two schools recently shut following attacks and abductions in the area. They are Mussa Junior and Primary School, which was shut after the abduction of more than 40 students and pupils, and Lassa Secondary School, which was also shut following the abduction of more than 30 students. The closures are a reminder of the long-running threat to education in Borno, where Boko Haram attacks have repeatedly targeted schools, teachers and students. The state government had previously ordered the temporary closure of schools in Mussa, Dille, Lassa and Chul communities in Askira-Uba for security reasons, while students writing examinations were moved to Government Secondary School, Uba. The Chairman of Askira-Uba LGA, Mada Saidu, had confirmed that 39 people, including three teaching staff and 36 students, were affected in one of the attacks. Borno was one of the states at the centre of the Safe Schools Initiative following the Chibok abduction in 2014. Plateau In Plateau State, insecurity has disrupted academic activities in Riyom and Barkin Ladi LGAs. Sunday Vanguard identified seven schools in the two LGAs affected by insecurity. They are Government Secondary School, GSS, Shonong, GSS Lwa, LEA Primary School, Hei-Gwe in Kwi District, GSS Fang, LEA Primary School Fang, all in Riyom LGA, as well as GSS Sho, GSS Barkin Ladi, GSS Ropp, Dogo Primary School, and LEA Primary School Dogo-Gashish in Barkin Ladi LGA.Berom Youth Moulders spokesman, Rwang Tenglong, said schools in affected communities were often shut for more than a week after attacks. He said insecurity had continued to undermine education in rural communities because schools could not operate effectively when communities were unsafe. Communities in Riyom where schools have experienced disruptions include Shonong, Lwa, Fang, Bangai, Tanjol, Darwat, Daku-Jol and Hei-Gwe Kwi. Kaduna Kaduna has generally maintained academic activities across most of its 23 LGAs, although some communities continue to experience insecurity. Sunday Vanguard identified two institutions in Chikun Local Government Area that have been affected by the security crisis: Bethel High School and Greenfield University. Their names remain associated with some of the most serious school abduction incidents recorded in the state. Birnin Gwari, Giwa, Chikun, Kajuru, Kauru and parts of Igabi continue to experience occasional disruptions arising from attacks, displacement and fears among parents and school authorities. Kebbi In Kebbi State, Government Girls Secondary School, Maga, in Danko/Wasagu Local Government Area, remains shut because of insecurity. The state government closed the school following a deadly attack and abduction of students by gunmen. The closure has further heightened concerns over the safety of boarding schools in communities vulnerable to attacks. Katsina In Katsina State, insecurity has led to prolonged closures of schools in several frontline LGAs. They include Batsari, Jibia, Kankara, Faskari, Sabuwa, Danmusa, Safana, Kurfi and Dandume. At the height of the crisis, schools in vulnerable communities were closed as a precautionary measure to protect pupils and teachers. Teachers were moved to safer communities while thousands of children were left without regular access to their schools. Education authorities responded by merging many affected schools with neighbouring institutions in safer communities. The arrangement has allowed thousands of pupils to continue learning, but several schools in frontline communities have yet to fully reopen because of lingering security concerns. Yobe Unlike Borno, Sunday Vanguard’s correspondent in Yobe reports that no school is currently shut because of insecurity except the College of Agriculture, Gujba. The state, however, remains deeply affected by the legacy of Boko Haram attacks on education. The College of Agriculture, Gujba, remains a reminder of the devastation caused by the insurgency. More than a decade after Boko Haram attacked the institution and killed students, the incident continues to symbolise the lasting consequences of attacks on educational institutions. The wider crisis The current Sunday Vanguard findings come against the background of a much larger national problem. A 2025 investigation separately documented at least 188 public schools shut because of insecurity across six northern states: Katsina, Benue, Zamfara, Niger, Sokoto and Kaduna. The breakdown put the number at 52 in Katsina, 55 in Benue, 39 in Zamfara, 30 in Niger, six in Sokoto and six in Kaduna. The investigation did not cover Borno, Yobe and Adamawa and noted that the actual number could be higher because some affected communities were inaccessible. The figure provides a wider picture of the scale and persistence of the education crisis. Maximum psychological impact Security experts said attacks across several states suggest that kidnapping and banditry are evolving, with criminals increasingly targeting schools, public officials and vulnerable communities. Security analyst, Sam Otoboeze, said the country’s kidnapping crisis was no longer driven solely by ransom payments but had also evolved into a strategy of intimidation designed to spread fear and undermine public confidence in the ability of the state to provide security. He said the growing frequency of attacks on schools and isolated communities showed that criminal groups were selecting targets capable of generating maximum psychological impact. Security consultant, Alfred Ononugbo, attributed the pattern partly to weak intelligence coordination and inadequate protection of vulnerable communities. He said once criminal groups discovered that communities, schools and rural settlements could be attacked with little resistance, they were likely to return to such locations or replicate the tactics elsewhere. Another security analyst, Masara Kim, described the situation as a major humanitarian and educational crisis, saying repeated attacks had devastated the education sector across the region. According to him, several schools, particularly LEA primary schools in Plateau, have either been shut down, destroyed or abandoned after their host communities were attacked and displaced. Kim cited LEA Primary School, Jwak in Mangu Local Government Area, which he said was completely burnt down during an attack on May 16, 2023, adding that the community remains deserted because residents have been unable to return due to insecurity. He disclosed that terrorists at one point occupied the government secondary school, the primary healthcare clinic and a church in Hawk community after residents fled the area. Kim further claimed that several children in Bokkos and Mangu were already out of school as of 2024 due to insecurity, warning that recent attacks, particularly in Mushere District where over 25,000 residents from more than 26 communities were displaced, may have pushed the number of out-of-school children in the two LGAs alone to over 40,000. Education experts warn of long-term damage The consequences of school closures extend beyond missed lessons, education experts warned. Chairman of the Conference of Polytechnics and Colleges of Technology in Nigeria, COREG, Dr Obini Onuchukwu, described the repeated closure of schools as one of the most damaging developments confronting the education sector. According to him, prolonged closures disrupt academic calendars and make it difficult for schools and institutions in affected areas to achieve the same educational outcomes as their counterparts in safer communities. He said students could not adequately compensate for prolonged classroom absence through private study at home, particularly where they lacked learning materials and proper supervision. Onuchukwu also warned of psychological consequences, saying prolonged exposure to violence and insecurity could produce emotional distress, mental trauma and loss of interest in education. He said attacks could also damage school facilities and disrupt the livelihoods of teachers, lecturers and other workers whose incomes depend on functioning educational institutions. He warned that the situation could further encourage young Nigerians to seek opportunities abroad. ‘We will lose a generation’ An educationist at the Delta State Institute of Continuing Education, Eloho Arhogho-Okeren, said school closures could have consequences long after schools reopen. “The closure of schools does more than halt lessons. It halts futures,” she said adding that some children who leave school temporarily never return, with many becoming involved in hawking, farming and other activities. She called for alternative learning through radio and community learning centres, alongside school feeding, transport support, financial assistance and accelerated learning programmes. “If we do not act now, we will not only lose a school year. We will lose a generation,” she said. ‘Out-of-school crisis could worsen’ Professor of Security Governance at the Federal University, Lafia, Dr Al Chukwuma Okoli, warned that prolonged school closures would worsen Nigeria’s already serious out-of-school problem. Okoli said Nigeria has an estimated 18.3 million out-of-school children and warned that school closures in conflict-affected communities could further increase the number. He said children who miss foundational learning opportunities face difficulties developing basic literacy and numeracy skills, leaving them vulnerable to functional illiteracy later in life. He added that prolonged disruption would also reduce the future employability of affected children, increasing their dependence on subsistence livelihoods. The girl-child, he said, faces additional risks, including child labour and early marriage. Okoli also warned of wider security implications, saying large populations of unschooled young people could become vulnerable to recruitment by terrorist groups, bandits and criminal networks. He described education disruption as a potential “threat multiplier” and called for urgent measures to protect and reopen schools. The lecturer recommended stronger early-warning systems, rapid response mechanisms, community-based protection, radio and television lessons, digital learning, conditional cash transfers and school feeding for displaced families. He also called for greater involvement of traditional and religious leaders in protecting schools and encouraging children to return to education. Psychological and social toll Speaking on the development, National President of the Association of Child and Learning Psychologists, Dr. Sixtus Unigwe, said effective and qualitative learning can only occur in an environment free from chaos and fear. He noted that children thrive physically, emotionally, socially and intellectually when they feel safe and loved, stressing that without a sense of security, learning becomes impossible. Unigwe explained that even when schools eventually reopen, the trauma from the initial closures is likely to linger. According to him, many pupils will struggle to concentrate in class, while others may develop truancy or avoid school entirely because it now feels threatening. “There is every tendency that the fear that led to the closure of schools will still be haunting some children,” he said, adding that a learning environment built on anxiety undermines academic performance and overall development. The psychologist further warned of broader societal consequences if the situation persists, saying children denied stable schooling may become vulnerable to gangsterism and other criminal activities including banditry and kidnapping. He described the potential impact as “devastating on the entire society,” and called for urgent measures to restore safety in schools to protect the future of children in the affected states. ActionAid seeks stronger implementation The Country Director of ActionAid Nigeria, Dr Andrew Mamedu, called for practical implementation of the Safe Schools Initiative and stronger protection of children in vulnerable communities. Mamedu said governments should provide alternative learning spaces for children displaced by insecurity and other emergencies. He also called for stronger implementation of the Safe Schools Declaration, particularly at community level. FG restructures Safe Schools Initiative The Federal Government says it is taking steps to strengthen the Safe Schools Initiative. Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, told the Senate Ad hoc Committee investigating the programme that the Ministry of Education had established a full-fledged Safe Schools Department. He said the ministry was working with the Office of the National Security Adviser, Department of State Services, Armed Forces, Nigeria Police Force and other security agencies to develop a comprehensive national framework for school safety. According to Alausa, the new approach would extend beyond physical security to include perimeter fencing, solar-powered lighting, water and sanitation facilities, school security personnel, technology and monitoring systems. “Safe Schools is much broader than physical security,” he said, stressing that central coordination was necessary because the initiative involved several agencies and levels of government. He said the Ministry of Education would provide policy direction, coordinate implementation with states and monitor the programme. “Today, the Safe Schools Initiative is officially domiciled in the Federal Ministry of Education. We have also established a dedicated Safe Schools Department to coordinate policy, implementation and monitoring,” he said. N144.8bn plan under scrutiny The Safe Schools Initiative has received substantial financial commitments since its creation, but continued attacks have raised questions about implementation and effectiveness. The initiative was launched in 2014 with an initial government commitment of $10 million, alongside private-sector funding. Subsequent fundraising pushed the resources mobilised for the initiative beyond $30 million. The Federal Government’s National Plan on Financing Safe Schools for 2023 to 2026 envisaged a further ¦ 144.86 billion investment. But the continued closure of schools has raised questions over how effectively the programme has translated financial commitments into physical protection for schools and communities. The Senate has consequently opened an investigation into the Safe Schools Initiative to examine its financial and operational performance. The inquiry comes as attacks continue to disrupt education in communities that remain vulnerable to terrorism and banditry. Education experts warn, every school forced to close represents another setback to the country’s struggle to build the skilled, educated population needed for economic growth and national security. Vanguard News The post Insecurity: Scores of schools in 40 LGAs shut down appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Fire extinguished at Aramco refinery in Jazan, Saudi Arabia says
items.description: Firefighters extinguished a fire that broke out early on Sunday at a facility at Aramco’s Jazan refinery in southwestern Saudi Arabia, the Saudi Energy Ministry said, adding that there were no injuries. Aramco’s industrial security teams had brought the fire under control and the relevant authorities were completing procedures to deal with the incident, the ministry said on X. It did not say what caused the fire. The Jazan refinery processes 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day and produces refined products including gasoline and ultra-light sulfur diesel. Aramco shut down the refinery on July 27 following an attack by Yemen’s Houthi rebels that damaged the plant’s Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle (IGCC) complex and tank farm area, according to a note from consultancy IIR seen by Reuters . The Houthis said at the time they had struck Aramco sites in Jazan and Yanbu. The attacks raised the prospect that threats to Red Sea shipping and Saudi oil infrastructure could widen global disruption stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran and Iranian attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz. Aramco chief Amin Nasser said last week that recent attacks on the company’s facilities had caused some production interruptions but that he was confident operations could be restored quickly. He said the attacks had no material operational or financial impact.

items.title: Tears, anger in Benue as 16 Otukpo attack victims buried
items.description: By Peter Duru, Makurdi Tears and anguish enveloped Efeyi community in Ugboju District of Otukpo Local Government Area, LGA, Benue State, on Saturday as residents conducted a mass burial for 16 persons allegedly killed by suspected armed herdsmen. The victims were reportedly killed when the attackers invaded the community in the early hours of July 28, throwing residents into panic and forcing many to flee for safety. According to residents, the assailants stormed Efeyi between 4am and 5am and opened fire on the community, killing 16 persons in what residents described as a brutal and unprovoked attack. The incident has heightened concerns over the security situation in the area, coming barely months after another deadly attack that claimed several lives in communities within the same district. At the mass burial, family members, community leaders, traditional rulers, political leaders and religious figures gathered to pay their final respects to the victims. The solemn ceremony was marked by grief as mourners struggled to hold back tears while the remains of the deceased were brought to the burial ground. A resident, Aboyi Owi, who attended the funeral, described the ceremony as one of the saddest moments in the history of the community. He said, “The funeral was so touching. The atmosphere is full of sorrow, tears and anger because this was an avoidable death if those responsible for ensuring the security of lives and property were alive to their responsibilities. “We do not know when our government will take genuine action to end the activities of armed herdsmen in this country. For as long as we allow armed herders to keep tormenting Nigerians, there will be no end to the mass killing of Nigerians by the criminal gangs. This is just the saddest day for the people of Efeyi community,” he added. Prayers were offered for the repose of the souls of the deceased as mourners observed moments of silence in honour of those who lost their lives in the attack. A Catholic priest led prayers at the ceremony before the coffins of the victims were lowered into the graves, amid wailing from bereaved relatives and sympathisers. The post Tears, anger in Benue as 16 Otukpo attack victims buried appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Police arrest Osun Commissioner over gunshots at APC rally; Adeleke kicks
items.description: By Shina Abubakar, OSOGBO The Police have arrested Osun State Commissioner for Environment, Mr Mayowa Asejoorin, in connection with gunshots fired at the All Progressives Congress, APC, holds rally in Ilesa on Saturday. Four persons were reportedly injured in the incident. Reacting, Governor Ademola Adeleke’s campaign team, The Imole Campaign Council, described the arrest as a plot to silence Accord leaders in the state. On the shooting, it was gathered that the APC supporters, during the rally in Ilesa metropolis, were attacked by some Accord chieftains, during which sporadic gunshots heard. As a result, people sustained different degrees of injury, including a 14-year-old Ilesanmi. As at press time, no casualty has been recorded. But the injured victims have been taken to the hospital for treatment. An eyewitness, Kola Adeoti disclosed that the boy was at his mother’s shop when he was hit by a stray bullet on his thigh. He added personnel of a security outfit based in the state, who escorted the Accord chieftains shot directly at the APC members which led to protest in Ilesa. Why we arrested him – Police Contacted, the Osun State Police Command spokesperson DSP Abiodun Ojelabi confirmed the report. He said the Commissioner for Environment, Mr Mayowa Asejoorin was arrested in connection with the incident. “Immediately the incident was reported, our personnel moved to the scene, cordoned off the area before some exhibit were recovered, which included expanded cartridges, Amotekun personnel caps. “Also, Mr Adejoorin was arrested the scene and has been taken to the command for questioning as part of the investigation process,” he added. Adeleke’s camp reacts Reacting, the Imole Campaign Council spokesman, Pelumi Olajengbesi, told newsmen at the Imole Media Centre on Saturday, in Osogbo, that the manner of arrest is particularly disturbing. He described the arrest as nothing short of a bandit-line abduction carried out under the cover of police authority. Olajengbesi called on the Inspector General of Police, Tunji Disu to reign in Osun Police Command and especially the Commissioner of Police, Ibrahim Gothan. He added that Accord leaders and members will not be intimidated, and that the will of the people can not be arrested. He said, “The latest victim of this alarming pattern is the Honourable Commissioner for Environment and Sanitation, Hon Mayowa Adejoorin, a prominent native of Ikiyinwa in Obokun Local Government Area of the state. “The manner of his arrest is particularly disturbing. We consider what happened to Hon Adejoorin nothing short of a bandit-line abduction carried out under the cover of police authority. “For some time now, we have witnessed a disturbing pattern in which prominent Accord leaders and supporters in Ijesaland are picked up by the Police on allegations that are apparently motivated by sinister political calculations, kept away from their families, communities and campaign activities, and thereby removed from circulation at a critical period of the electoral process. ‘APC desperate’ “The APC is desperate in Ijesaland. And rather than face the people in a free, fair and competitive election, there is a growing concern that these rejected political actors may be seeking to weaken the Accord Party’s structures by removing its leaders from the field. “We are therefore deeply concerned that these arrests may be connected to an attempt to create an environment conducive to electoral manipulation in Ijesaland ahead of the August 15 governorship election. “We therefore call directly on the Inspector-General of Police, Mr Tunde Disu, to urgently intervene in the situation in Osun State. “Mr Inspector-General, the buck stops at your table. We call on you to rein in the Osun State Police Command and Mr Gottan in particular and immediately investigate the disturbing pattern of arrests involving Accord leaders, particularly in Ijesaland. “We demand answers. On what basis was Hon Mayowa Adejoorin arrested? What offence has he committed? What evidence exists against him? Why was his arrest carried out in such a manner? And why does the Police appear increasingly willing to deploy its powers only against Accord political leaders at this critical moment in our democratic process? “We demand the immediate release of Hon Mayowa Adejoorin, as we believe, there is no lawful and credible basis for his abduction and detention.” Vanguard News The post Police arrest Osun Commissioner over gunshots at APC rally; Adeleke kicks appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Tucker Carlson : « Il est temps de sauver l’Amérique » (discours intégral)
items.description: Le 5 août 2026, à quatre-vingt-dix jours des élections de mi-mandat , Tucker Carlson a diffusé sur sa plateforme un monologue d'environ deux heures, intitulé sobrement : « It's Time to Save America » (Il est temps de sauver l’Amérique), accompagnant la publication d'un manifeste en dix points. Ce discours attendu avait été annoncé quatre jours plus tôt par l'ancienne représentante trumpiste Marjorie Taylor Greene, photographiée en réunion avec Carlson, le représentant du Kentucky Thomas Massie et Joe Kent, directeur démissionnaire du Centre national du contre-terrorisme. « Nous avions dit : plus de guerres étrangères, et nous le pensions. Nous avons soutenu Donald Trump parce qu'il en avait fait la promesse. Mais il nous a tous trahis. Notre engagement, c'est l'Amérique d'abord, pour tous les Américains, à droite, à gauche et au centre. Le mouvement a commencé. » Le discours vise à marquer la rupture avec la base national-populiste de Donald Trump et les grandes orientations de son second mandat. À Washington, la riposte a été immédiate. La Maison-Blanche a moqué « une collection embarrassante de renégats geignards qui surestiment considérablement leur influence et leur pertinence » 6 , en rappelant que Trump demeure le « chef incontesté » du Parti républicain. Le président lui-même répète depuis le printemps que Carlson « a perdu son chemin » et qu’il « n’est pas MAGA ». Ce dernier assume désormais ouvertement la rupture : « Nous avons besoin d’options… Je vais aider à construire un troisième parti. » C'est autour de ce diagnostic que cette personnalité extrême cherche à faire converger plusieurs lignes critiques traversant la société américaine. Selon lui, ce système serait capturé par une « classe Epstein », dominée par deux partis « identiques » sur l'essentiel (la guerre, le budget et l'impôt), et incapable de répondre aux deux menaces qui pèsent sur l'humanité : une guerre nucléaire résultant de la fusion des conflits en Ukraine et en Iran, et l'explosion de l'intelligence artificielle. Il est également Si l’impasse de la guerre en Iran est le symptôme d’une « trahison », c'est dans l'affaire Epstein et dans le rôle d'Israël dans la politique américaine que l'ancienne star de Fox News cherche à créer une division, sur fond de banalisation de l'antisémitisme dans une partie de la droite américaine abreuvée de contenus de Nick Fuentes et d’ IA négationnistes . L’objectif de Carlson est d'obtenir un changement systémique. Il s'agit d'un « changement de régime » intérieur, obtenu par la création d'un troisième parti qui, en divisant le vote conservateur, pourrait priver le président de sa majorité dès le mois de novembre, alors que 43 % des électeurs se disent insatisfaits des deux grands partis New York Times /Siena College , réalisé en mai 2026 auprès des électeurs inscrits et publié le 29 mai 2026.'> 7 . Le décalogue de Tucker Carlson vise à ouvrir une nouvelle phase du national-populisme aux États-Unis, en redéfinissant une doctrine trumpiste après l'ère Trump. Pour accompagner notre analyse de la recomposition de la scène politique américaine, nous traduisons et commentons ce discours important, souvent incohérent et brouillon, en le commentant presque ligne à ligne. Le but de tout système est de protéger les intérêts des personnes qu’il sert et qu’il gouverne. C’est tout simplement dans sa nature. Ainsi, quel est le rôle d’un prédicateur ? C’est de s’occuper des âmes de ses fidèles. Quel est le rôle d’un président ? C’est de veiller aux intérêts de ses citoyens et de les protéger. C’est vraiment simple. C’est inhérent à la définition même de ces fonctions. Il est donc évident, depuis un certain temps déjà, que notre système ne fonctionne pas comme prévu, car ceux qui en sont responsables semblent veiller principalement – pas exclusivement, mais principalement – à leurs propres intérêts. On le constate partout autour de soi : les fonctionnaires gagnent plus que l’Américain moyen. Cela en dit long. On le constate à tous les niveaux des institutions de la vie américaine : beaucoup d’entre elles semblent fonctionner avant tout au profit de ceux qui les dirigent. Et c’est grave. Et ils s’en cachent moins que jamais. Ils s’offrent des îles privées et se croient exempts des règles qui s’appliquent à vous. Cela a provoqué une énorme frustration et un profond ressentiment chez les gens ordinaires : « Attendez une seconde, vous ne respectez pas vos propres règles. Je dois rester chez moi pendant la pandémie de COVID, pendant que vous, vous allez au French Laundry… Vous vous prenez pour quoi exactement, un roi ? » Effectivement, la réponse est oui. La construction de cet argument unit deux temporalités différentes. Le paradigme évoqué est le dîner de Gavin Newsom au restaurant trois étoiles French Laundry de la Napa Valley, le 6 novembre 2020, en pleine période de restrictions, qui est devenu le symbole de l'hypocrisie sanitaire des élites. En évoquant un événement vieux de six ans, plutôt que les affaires du second mandat de Trump, Carlson installe d’emblée la thèse du discours. La corruption serait celle d'un « système » bipartisan, et non d'un camp. On assiste donc à une dégradation très évidente d’un système, qui devient de plus en plus corrompu avec le temps, et ceux qui détiennent le pouvoir l’utilisent à leur propre profit, ainsi qu’à celui de leur famille et de leurs amis. On a fini par appeler ça la « classe Epstein », parce que c’est exactement ce que c’est. L'expression « classe Epstein » n'est pas de Carlson. Apparue à la fin de l'année 2025 dans le contexte de la bataille autour des Epstein Files , elle a été introduite dans le discours politique par le démocrate californien Ro Khanna, membre de la Chambre des représentants des États-Unis, puis reprise par le sénateur de Géorgie et ancien producteur de documentaires Jon Ossoff, ainsi que par la droite et l’extrême droite national-populiste. Elle désigne un réseau transpartisan d'élites jouissant d'une impunité de fait. L'affaire fournit un langage commun aux deux populismes, et c'est au cœur de ce clivage que Carlson cherche à se positionner. C’est un groupe de personnes égoïstes agissant dans leur propre intérêt, au détriment du vôtre. C’est entendu. C’est certes extrêmement néfaste, mais ça peut perdurer pendant très longtemps parce que c’est tout simplement la nature même des systèmes. C’est comme l’Empire ottoman, qui avait conquis la moitié du monde et qui est passé à un état plutôt pathétique, en ne se concentrant plus que sur son harem. Pour, finalement, se dissoudre. Quelque chose de différent est arrivé à notre système. C’est devenu évident ces derniers temps : c’est une chose d’avoir un système dirigé par des gens qui veillent à leurs propres intérêts et non aux vôtres — nous avons déjà connu cela ; c’en est une autre d’avoir un système totalement incapable de réagir à la réalité, pratiquement paralysé. Malheureusement, et de manière très inquiétante, c’est le système dont nous disposons aujourd’hui. Nous le savons parce que les deux plus grandes menaces, sans doute, de toute l’histoire connue, à savoir la guerre nucléaire et l’IA, se profilent juste devant nous. Tout le discours repose sur cette prémisse catastrophiste ancrée dans l'imaginaire de la décadence et du déclin , qui est également central dans la construction de l'imaginaire d'extrême droite. Le procédé consiste à hisser l'intelligence artificielle au rang de la guerre nucléaire afin de rendre l'inaction des élites face aux menaces « existentielles » d'autant plus condamnable. Et personne dans notre société occupant un poste d’autorité ne semble capable de réagir, ni même de reconnaître réellement que cela est en train de se produire. C’est comme s’ils étaient figés, les yeux rivés sur l’arbre qui fonce vers le pare-brise à 70 miles à l’heure. C’est vraiment l’impression que l’on a. Si vous écoutez attentivement, c’est exactement là où nous en sommes. Nous nous dirigeons donc, si cette trajectoire se maintient, vers un conflit nucléaire, car deux conflits – l’un au Moyen-Orient et l’autre en Europe de l’Est, en Ukraine et en Iran – sont soudainement en train de se confondre d’une manière ou d’une autre. Si les deux conflits sont pour l'instant connectés marginalement , aucun élément public ne laisse penser qu'un recours à l'arme nucléaire ait été envisagé par Washington contre l'Iran. Cette « prédiction » procède par extrapolation à partir de faits réels, comme l'enlisement du conflit, pour faire déduire une escalade « inévitable » vers l'arme atomique. Ce glissement du plausible au certain est l'un des ressorts rhétoriques du discours. Qu’est-ce que cela signifie ? Cela signifie une guerre mondiale. La Russie livre à l'Iran des drones Shahed améliorés, inversant ainsi la tendance de 2022, et lui fournirait également des renseignements satellitaires sur les forces américaines. Le 25 juillet, l'Ukraine a frappé un cargo iranien en mer Caspienne, accusé d'approvisionner la Russie, ce qui constitue le premier accrochage direct entre Kiev et Téhéran. Le saut de cette connexion réelle à « une guerre mondiale » entre deux camps constitués reste une interprétation typique de la rhétorique escalatoire de Carlson. Et vous avez deux camps aux positions fondamentalement inflexibles. Sans entrer dans les détails, si vous suivez cette actualité, si vous faites partie du petit pourcentage d’Américains qui la suivent, vous savez déjà qu’il n’y a pas de résolution évidente à l’un ou l’autre de ces conflits dans un avenir proche, et que pourtant les enjeux ne pourraient pas être plus cruciaux. Bien sûr, les principaux acteurs de ces deux guerres, qui ne font désormais plus qu’une, sont dotés de l’arme nucléaire. Ils estiment que cela est, pour employer un terme très galvaudé, une question existentielle pour eux. Ainsi, à moins que l’angle d’attaque et la trajectoire sur laquelle nous sommes ne changent très rapidement, nous allons inévitablement aboutir à l’utilisation d’armes de destruction massive. L’un des protagonistes, le président des États-Unis, le menace déjà ouvertement sur Truth Social, sur Internet, aux yeux de tous : « Nous allons anéantir votre civilisation. » On ne peut pas faire cela avec des Tomahawks, c’est évident, mais on peut le faire avec des armes nucléaires. Le président des États-Unis, quoi qu’on vous dise, menace ouvertement de recourir aux armes nucléaires dans un conflit qui n’a pas de résolution immédiate ni évidente. Dans un message publié sur Truth Social le 7 avril 2026, quelques heures avant un énième ultimatum concernant la réouverture du détroit d'Ormuz, il affirmait : « Une civilisation entière va mourir ce soir, pour ne jamais revenir. Je ne veux pas que cela arrive, mais cela arrivera probablement. » Ces menaces apocalyptiques ont pu suggérer un signal nucléaire, mais Trump n'a jamais mentionné l'arme atomique à ce sujet. La mise en cause frontale et explicite du président (que Carlson avait pourtant critiqué dans des messages privés révélés par la presse) témoigne de l'ampleur de la rupture. Alors, où cela mène-t-il ? Vers une frappe nucléaire. Quant à ce qui se passera ensuite, Dieu seul le sait. Mais si vous pouvez ne serait-ce que vivre avec ce fait, si vous pouvez ne serait-ce que dire ou simplement reconnaître sans le formuler que, oui, cela pourrait aboutir à ce que des gens lancent des armes nucléaires sur des populations civiles, vous avez déjà perdu la tête. Vous vous êtes déjà montré incapable d’exercer un leadership, car c’est de la folie. C’est bien plus qu’une imprudence. C’est… c’est littéralement… suicidaire et meurtrier. Et à tout le moins, vous êtes paralysé. Vous êtes incapable d’agir pour vous défendre, pas seulement pour défendre votre pays ou votre civilisation, mais même pour vous défendre vous-même. C’est là où nous en sommes. Il en va de même pour l’IA. Bien sûr, on ne sait pas, tout comme pour les guerres en Ukraine et en Iran, où l’IA va nous mener. Peut-être s’agit-il simplement d’une énorme bulle. Vous savez, c’est la bulle technologique de 2000. C’est Pets.com multiplié par 100. Peut-être qu’à l’inverse, les prédictions de ceux qui développent cette technologie s’avéreront vraies, à savoir que ce sera la fin. Au mieux, nous abandonnons notre capacité à prendre des décisions importantes concernant notre vie au profit des machines ; nous confions nos vies à des machines. C’est le meilleur des cas. Dans le pire des cas, les machines décident de tous nous tuer et passent à l’acte, sans que nous puissions rien y faire. C’est ce qu’ils disent. Pas les prophètes de l’apocalypse sur Twitter, mais bien les individus qui développent cette technologie : « Oh, au fait, ce truc qu’on est en train de créer pourrait tuer tout le monde et, au minimum, il fera en sorte que vos enfants, vos petits-enfants et probablement vous-mêmes n’ayez plus d’emploi. » En mai 2023, les dirigeants d'OpenAI, d'Anthropic et de Google DeepMind signaient une déclaration du Center for AI Safety dans laquelle ils plaçaient le « risque d'extinction » lié à l'IA au même niveau que les pandémies et la guerre nucléaire. En mai 2025, Dario Amodei prédisait la disparition de « la moitié de tous les emplois de cols blancs débutants dans les 1 à 5 prochaines années ». Il y a quelques jours a été publié un autre texte intitulé Pacing the Frontier et signé par plus d'un millier d'ingénieurs de laboratoires de pointe, dont Amodei et le directeur scientifique d'OpenAI, Jakub Pachocki, pour demander à Washington de se doter des moyens de « ralentir délibérément » la course à l'IA. L'originalité de Carlson consiste à retourner ce catastrophisme managérial, dont on peut également analyser la dimension marketing, en réquisitoire populiste contre ceux-là mêmes qui le professent. On va, j’imagine, faire quelque chose pour y remédier. Mais on ne sait pas trop quoi, et ça va arriver d’ici un an environ. Ce qui est remarquable, ce n’est pas seulement que ceux qui s’en occupent l’admettent, ni qu’ils essaient vraiment d’attirer notre attention en nous disant : « C’est ce que nous sommes en train de faire. » Mais c’est que personne ne fasse quoi que ce soit. Tous paraissent simplement hypnotisés, le regard rivé sur cette chose qui pourrait bien signifier la fin de tout. Qui se comporte de cette façon ? Les gens normaux ne se comportent pas ainsi, et les systèmes fonctionnels, certainement pas non plus. Donc, sans m’étendre sur le sujet, qu’est-ce que cela nous dit ? Cela nous indique que le système a atteint ses limites. Ce n’est en réalité pas un système qui fonctionne dans l’intérêt de qui que ce soit. C’est un système voué à une destruction probablement assez imminente. Il est donc en train de disparaître. On savait sans doute déjà que tout système qui permet d'élire des octogénaires pour diriger le pays, des octogénaires cyniques, n’en a plus pour longtemps. Trump vient de fêter ses 80 ans à la Maison-Blanche lors d'une soirée avec des combats MMA , tandis que Biden a quitté ses fonctions à l'âge de 82 ans. Carlson retourne ainsi contre Trump l'argument de l'âge et du déclin, que le camp MAGA avait utilisé contre Biden en 2024, l'un des tabous les plus stricts du trumpisme. Si les « octogénaires cyniques » visent les deux présidents sans les nommer, ils s'inscrivent dans une contestation de plus en plus forte de « l'oligarchie boomer » aux États-Unis, qui a ciblé des figures comme Nancy Pelosi (dont l'annonce du retrait, en novembre 2025 à 85 ans, a relancé la guerre générationnelle chez les démocrates) ou Mitch McConnell, 84 ans, qui ne briguera pas de nouveau mandat au Sénat après ses épisodes d'absence en public. Un tel système ne peut pas se reproduire, de la même manière que les octogénaires ne se reproduisent pas. C’est la fin : c’est bien le cas et c’est triste. On a certainement passé beaucoup de temps à s’en plaindre. Mais, à ce stade, c’est tout simplement une évidence. Il vaut donc la peine de réfléchir à ce qui va suivre, en supposant que nous soyons tous encore là — il faut partir de ce principe, car c’est certainement ce que vous souhaitez et, même si ce n’est pas le cas, il faut quand même s’y préparer, car on ne sait jamais. Quelque chose va se passer ensuite, quelque chose qui remplacera le système. On peut espérer que ce remplacement, quel qu’il soit, soit le résultat d’un processus progressif que les gens auront le temps d’assimiler, d’accepter et d’approuver, pour qu’on n’ait pas de changement brusque, car les changements brusques de direction politique sont… Eh bien, on les appelle des révolutions. Et elles ne constituent généralement pas une amélioration par rapport à ce qu’elles remplacent. Elles ont leurs propres inconvénients. On espère donc que cela évoluera d’une manière ou d’une autre vers quelque chose de moins fou, de moins éloigné de la mission première d’un système, qui est de servir les gens qui vivent ici, et de plus humain et de plus favorable à l’humain, etc. Que ce soit tout simplement mieux à tous égards. C’est ce qu’on espère. Mais quoi qu’il en soit, on va vers quelque chose de différent. La question est : qu’est-ce que ce sera ? On ne le sait pas. On sait que les évolutions technologiques ou les changements de rapport de force à l’échelle mondiale, tous ces faits constatés sur le terrain, s’accompagnent et sont suivis de changements politiques. Ici, le cadre évoqué par Carlson est matérialiste. La politique ne serait qu'une « réponse » aux basculements technologiques et géopolitiques. Cette vision permet de présenter la fin du système non pas comme un programme, mais comme une fatalité qu'il suffirait d'accompagner. Ironie du sort, l'expression « changement de régime », que Carlson abhorre en politique étrangère, devient sa prophétie en politique intérieure. Les changements politiques découlent de ces évolutions. Ils ne les provoquent pas, mais ce sont des réponses à ces évolutions. Nous assistons donc à des changements politiques, appelés à trouver une expression politique. Sera-ce un troisième parti ? Probablement. Le constat le plus radical qu’on peut faire sur la politique américaine au cours du dernier siècle, et nous en avons eu la confirmation le 28 février, c’est que les partis ont des positionnements similaires sur les grandes questions. Avec l'opération Epic Fury déclenchée le 28 février, les États-Unis et Israël ont franchi un seuil sans précédent. Des frappes massives et coordonnées contre l'Iran, un objectif de changement de régime assumé publiquement par Trump et l'élimination du Guide suprême, Ali Khamenei. Pour le mouvement MAGA construit en partie sur le rejet des « guerres sans fin », le désengagement du Moyen-Orient et la critique des politiques de « regime change », la date marque une rupture et forme un paradigme. Côté offre politique, la cassure est immédiate. Que signifie être américain ? On peut y remédier. Il suffit d’essayer et nous allons essayer. Nous vous tiendrons au courant au fur et à mesure que nous poursuivrons cette démarche. Après dix principes formulés dans un langage universel (l'équité, les droits, la décence), le discours aborde « l'identité américaine » comme une « question urgente » et un programme (« nous allons essayer »). C'est la clef de voûte d'un texte que la presse américaine lit comme le manifeste d'une recomposition à venir : un troisième parti ou une refondation du national-populisme qu'a été le trumpisme, sans Trump ou après lui. Merci de votre écoute. L’article Tucker Carlson : « Il est temps de sauver l’Amérique » (discours intégral) est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .
